tamil:
செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான் சினங்காப்பான் அல்லிடத்துக்
காக்கின்என் காவாக்கா லென்.
transliteration:
Sellidaththuk kaappaan sinangaappaan allidaththuk
Kaakkin en kaavaakkaal en.
current_meaning: The one who truly restrains anger is the one who holds it back where it could actually take effect and do harm. Where anger has no power to act anyway, what difference does it make whether you hold it back or not?
elementary_explanation: Imagine a big kid who could easily push a small kid, but chooses not to. That is real self-control. If a small kid can't push a big kid anyway, 'not pushing' isn't really a choice. This kural says being calm only counts when you really could have hurt someone and you don't.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter by redefining the virtue itself: restraint of anger (sinam kaaththal) is morally meaningful only where one has the power (sellidam, literally 'the place where it goes through') to make the anger effective. Classical commentators such as Parimelazhagar read sellidam as the case of anger toward those weaker than oneself, where retaliation would succeed; restraint toward the stronger is mere prudence or fear. The couplet thus locates virtue in the gap between capacity and action, anticipating the Aristotelian and Stoic view that a virtue is shown only where its opposite is genuinely available. The rhetorical question of the second line ('what if he guards it, what if he does not?') dismisses 'restraint' that costs nothing as morally empty.

tamil:
செல்லா இடத்துச் சினந்தீது செல்லிடத்தும்
இல்அதனின் தீய பிற.
transliteration:
Sellaa idaththuch sinandheedhu sellidaththum
Il adhanin theeya pira.
current_meaning: Anger where it cannot take effect (against those stronger than you) is harmful to yourself. And where it can take effect (against those weaker than you), there is nothing more evil than it.
elementary_explanation: If you get angry at a much bigger kid, you will probably get hurt. If you get angry at a much smaller kid, you might hurt them, and that is even worse. So anger is bad either way: it hurts you, or it makes you hurt someone who can't fight back.
university_explanation: This couplet completes the argument of 301 by closing every escape route: anger is bad where it is ineffective (sellaa idam, anger toward the powerful, which rebounds on oneself) and worst of all where it is effective (sellidam, anger toward the weak, which inflicts real injury). Mu. Varadarasanar's gloss makes the two cases explicit as 'stronger' and 'weaker' persons. The ethical weight falls on the second line: power over others magnifies the moral gravity of anger rather than licensing it. The structure anticipates modern concerns about abuse of authority in households, workplaces, and states, where anger combined with power becomes cruelty.

tamil:
மறத்தல் வெகுளியை யார்மாட்டும் தீய
பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும்.
transliteration:
Maraththal vekuliyai yaarmaattum theeya
Piraththal adhanaan varum.
current_meaning: Let go of anger toward anyone at all, and forget it, for every kind of evil is born from anger.
elementary_explanation: Anger is like a seed that grows weeds. If you keep it, bad things grow out of it: mean words, fights, broken friendships. So the kural says: let go of anger, no matter who made you angry.
university_explanation: The verb maraththal ('forgetting', 'letting go') is significant: Valluvar does not ask merely for suppression but for the anger to be dropped from memory, since resentment that is stored continues to generate harm. Yaarmaattum ('toward anyone whatsoever') universalises the precept, removing the distinctions of power drawn in 301 and 302. The second line offers a causal claim: evils (theeya) are 'born' (piraththal) from anger, making it a root vice rather than one fault among many. This genealogical view of anger as a source of other wrongs parallels the Buddhist treatment of dosa as one of the three roots of unwholesome action and the Gita's chain from desire to anger to ruin.

tamil:
நகையும் உவகையும் கொல்லும் சினத்தின்
பகையும் உளவோ பிற.
transliteration:
Nagaiyum uvagaiyum kollum sinaththin
Pagaiyum ulavo pira.
current_meaning: Anger kills both the smile on the face and the joy in the heart. Is there any enemy greater than that?
elementary_explanation: When you are really angry, you can't laugh and you can't feel happy. It's like a thief that steals your smile. The kural asks: what enemy could be worse than one that takes away all your happiness?
university_explanation: Valluvar pairs nagai (laughter, the outward cheerfulness of the face) with uvagai (inner delight), a pairing the commentators render as 'face-blossoming and heart-blossoming'. Anger 'kills' both, so the damage is not only social but inward. The rhetorical question reframes anger as a pagai (enemy) that lives within, which is more dangerous than any external foe because it cannot be escaped. The idea of anger as an internal enemy runs through Indian thought (the 'six inner enemies', including krodha) and has close parallels in the Buddhist teaching that an angry person does to himself what an enemy would wish on him.

tamil:
தன்னைத்தான் காக்கின் சினங்காக்க காவாக்கால்
தன்னையே கொல்லுஞ் சினம்.
transliteration:
Thannaiththaan kaakkin sinangaakka kaavaakkaal
Thannaiye kollum sinam.
current_meaning: If you want to protect yourself, guard against anger. If you do not guard against it, anger will destroy you yourself.
elementary_explanation: Anger is like a fire you carry in your own pocket. If you don't put it out, it burns you first. So the best way to keep yourself safe is to keep anger away.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on the reflexive thannai ('oneself'), which frames it: the whole argument is about self-preservation, not the protection of others. Valluvar's point is strategic as much as moral: anger, left unguarded, turns back on its owner, destroying health, judgment, reputation, and eventually life. The repetition of kaa ('guard') across both lines makes guarding anger identical with guarding the self. This self-interested argument against anger complements the altruistic ones elsewhere in the chapter and matches Stoic and Buddhist analyses that anger harms its owner before its target.

tamil:
சினமென்னும் சேர்ந்தாரைக் கொல்லி இனமென்னும்
ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும்.
transliteration:
Sinamennum serndhaaraik kolli inamennum
Emap punaiyaich sudum.
current_meaning: Anger is a fire that kills whoever comes near it, and it burns up even the raft of kinsmen and friends that would carry a person safely through life.
elementary_explanation: Think of your family and friends as a raft that keeps you floating in a big river. Anger is like a fire on that raft. If you let it burn, it destroys the very thing that keeps you safe.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a compound metaphor. Sinam is called serndhaaraik kolli, 'the killer of those who come close', a traditional kenning for fire, which destroys whatever touches it. Inam, one's kin and circle of friends, is called an emap punai, a 'safe raft' that carries one across the dangerous sea of life. Anger, being fire, burns the very raft that was meant to save its owner: it isolates the angry person by consuming the relationships that sustain them. Valluvar thus extends the self-harm argument of 305 to its social dimension.

tamil:
சினத்தைப் பொருளென்று கொண்டவன் கேடு
நிலத்தறைந்தான் கைபிழையா தற்று.
transliteration:
Sinaththaip porulendru kondavan kedu
Nilaththaraindhaan kai pizhaiyaadhatru.
current_meaning: Ruin will surely come to the person who treats anger as something valuable, just as surely as the hand of a person who strikes the ground cannot escape being hurt.
elementary_explanation: If you slap the floor as hard as you can, the floor doesn't feel anything, but your hand really hurts. Using anger as your 'power' is the same: the person who uses it gets hurt the most.
university_explanation: The target here is a specific attitude: treating anger as porul, a thing of worth or a useful tool, whether as a mark of strength, a way to command respect, or a means of getting results. The simile of striking the ground (nilaththu araindhaan) is precise: the ground is unharmed while the striker's hand is certain to be injured, so anger's force rebounds on its user. Kai pizhaiyaadhu ('the hand does not escape') stresses certainty, not mere probability. The couplet enters a long-running debate, found in Aristotle and Seneca, about whether anger is a useful servant of virtue; Valluvar sides firmly with those who deny it any value.

tamil:
இணர்எரி தோய்வன்ன இன்னா செயினும்
புணரின் வெகுளாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Inar eri thoivanna innaa seyinum
Punarin vekulaamai nandru.
current_meaning: Even if someone does you harm as painful as being plunged into a blazing fire, it is good, if you possibly can, to refrain from anger toward them.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes people are so mean it feels like being burned. The kural says: even then, if you can, try not to become angry back. It is really hard, but it is the best and bravest thing to do.
university_explanation: This is the chapter's high-water mark of demand: inar eri, a fire of many clustered flames, is the image of the worst possible injury. The concessive punarin ('if it is possible', or in some readings 'if the offender seeks reconciliation') is realistic, acknowledging that non-anger in such extremity may exceed ordinary capacity, but it does not lower the ideal. Kalaignar's gloss takes punarin as the wrongdoer returning to seek friendship, making the couplet about accepting reconciliation without resentment. Either way, the teaching approaches the most radical ethics of non-retaliation found across traditions.

tamil:
உள்ளிய தெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும் உள்ளத்தால்
உள்ளான் வெகுளி எனின்.
transliteration:
Ulliyadhellaam udaneydhum ullaththaal
Ullaan vekuli enin.
current_meaning: If a person never lets even the thought of anger enter the mind, he will attain at once everything he sets his heart on.
elementary_explanation: When your mind isn't full of angry thoughts, it has lots of room for good ideas and plans. People also like to help calm, kind people. So a mind without anger can reach its goals much more easily.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on the root ul- ('to think', 'the mind'): ulliyadhu ('what one has thought of'), ullaththaal ('in the mind'), and ullaan ('does not think of'). Valluvar sets the standard at the level of thought itself: it is not enough to avoid angry acts or words; one must not entertain (ullaan) anger inwardly. The promised reward, attaining all one intends 'at once' (udan), is striking, and commentators variously read it as worldly success (a clear mind and goodwill from others) or spiritual attainment. The couplet thus links inner purity from anger to efficacy in the world, a pattern also found in the Gita's promise of liberation for those free of desire and anger.

tamil:
இறந்தார் இறந்தார் அனையர் சினத்தைத்
துறந்தார் துறந்தார் துணை.
transliteration:
Irandhaar irandhaar anaiyar sinaththaith
Thurandhaar thurandhaar thunai.
current_meaning: Those who go beyond all bounds in anger are no better than the dead. Those who have wholly renounced anger are equal to those who have renounced the world.
elementary_explanation: A person who is always furious is like someone who isn't really alive: there's no joy, kindness, or peace inside. But a person who has given up anger is like a wise holy person. Letting go of anger makes you truly alive.
university_explanation: The closing couplet is a celebrated piece of Tamil wordplay built on two repeated verbs. Irandhaar can mean 'those who have exceeded (all limits)' and 'those who have died'; thurandhaar can mean 'those who have renounced (anger)' and 'those who have renounced (the world)', that is, ascetics. Hence: the excessively angry are like the dead; those who give up anger equal the renunciants. Solomon Pappaiah's gloss offers an alternative reading, that those free of anger are like those who have escaped death, which neatly mirrors the first line. Placed in the Thuravaraviyal (the section on ascetic virtue), the couplet makes giving up anger itself a form of renunciation available to everyone.

tamil:
சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும் பிறர்க்குஇன்னா
செய்யாமை மாசற்றார் கோள்.
transliteration:
Sirappeenum selvam perinum pirarkku innaa
Seyyaamai maasatraar kol.
current_meaning: Even if hurting someone would win them wealth great enough to bring honour and prestige, people whose minds are free of stain hold firmly to the rule of never causing pain to others.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone offers you a huge treasure chest, but only if you push another kid down to get it. A truly good person says “no thanks” every time. Valluvar says the pure-hearted never hurt anyone, not even for the biggest prize in the world.
university_explanation: The chapter opens by testing the principle of non-harm against its strongest temptation: sirappu eenum selvam, wealth that “gives birth to” distinction and social standing. The word kol (settled principle, fixed resolve) matters: non-harm is presented not as a mood or a calculation but as a standing commitment of the maasatraar, “those without stain,” whose minds are clear of the anger and greed that make harm seem attractive. Placed in the turavaraviyal (the section on the renunciant’s virtues), the couplet implies that the refusal to profit from another’s suffering is a defining mark of spiritual maturity, not merely of good manners. The same structure appears in Cicero’s Stoic claim that profiting by a neighbour’s loss is more contrary to nature than death or poverty, and in Plato’s thought-experiment of the Ring of Gyges, which asks whether anyone would stay just if injustice were profitable and safe. Valluvar’s answer is that the stainless would.

tamil:
கறுத்துஇன்னா செய்தவக் கண்ணும் மறுத்தின்னா
செய்யாமை மாசற்றார் கோள்.
transliteration:
Karuththu innaa seydhavak kannum maruththu innaa
Seyyaamai maasatraar kol.
current_meaning: Even when someone, out of spite, has done them harm, the stainless make it their rule not to hurt that person in return.
elementary_explanation: If a kid on the playground knocks over your sandcastle on purpose, it is tempting to knock over theirs too. This kural says good-hearted people don’t pay back hurt with more hurt, even when the other person started it.
university_explanation: Where Kural 311 tested non-harm against greed, 312 tests it against the stronger pull of justified grievance. Karuththu describes the other party’s grudging, hostile intent, while maruththu (in return, in retort) names the retaliatory impulse the stainless decline. The couplet repeats the closing phrase of 311 word for word (seyyaamai maasatraar kol), binding the two into a pair: neither profit nor provocation licenses harm. This places Valluvar alongside Socrates in the Crito, who startled his friend by insisting that one must not return injury for injury, and alongside the Sermon on the Mount and the Buddha’s Simile of the Saw. It also stands in contrast to the older Greek ethic of helping friends and harming enemies, which Plato’s Socrates set out to dismantle.

tamil:
செய்யாமல் செற்றார்க்கும் இன்னாத செய்தபின்
உய்யா விழுமந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Seyyaamal setraarkkum innaadha seydhapin
Uyyaa vizhumam tharum.
current_meaning: Even toward people who hated and harmed you when you had done nothing to them, if you strike back with harm, it will afterwards bring you sorrow you cannot escape.
elementary_explanation: Suppose someone is mean to you for no reason at all, and you get them back. It might feel fair for a minute, but later you end up feeling awful and stuck in a big fight. The kural says hitting back, even when you didn’t start it, brings trouble you can’t get out of.
university_explanation: This couplet sharpens 312 by removing every excuse: the victim did nothing (seyyaamal) to provoke the enmity (setraar, those who hate). Even so, retaliating yields uyyaa vizhumam, a grief from which there is no escape. Because the chapter belongs to the section on the renunciant, older commentators and Pope’s translation read it as addressed to the ascetic, for whom retaliation undoes the discipline of years; the ‘inescapable sorrow’ is at once moral self-damage and the karmic consequence of the act. The logic is prudential as well as ethical: revenge draws the avenger into the cycle of harm. Greek tragedy dramatises exactly this spiral in the house of Atreus, and the Gospel compresses it into the saying that those who take the sword perish by it.

tamil:
இன்னாசெய் தாரை ஒறுத்தல் அவர்நாண
நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்.
transliteration:
Innaa seydhaarai oruththal avar naana
Nannayam seydhu vidal.
current_meaning: The true way to punish those who have harmed you is to do them such kindness that they feel ashamed, and then to let the matter go.
elementary_explanation: If your brother breaks your toy and you share your snack with him anyway, he will probably feel really sorry about the toy. Valluvar says that is the best “punishment”: being so kind that the person feels ashamed of being mean, and then forgetting about it.
university_explanation: Perhaps the most quoted couplet of the chapter, 314 redefines punishment itself. Oruththal (to punish, chastise) is kept as the goal, but the means is nannayam (goodness, benefit), and its effect is naanam, the wrongdoer’s shame. The closing word vidal (to leave off, let go) led Parimelazhagar and later commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan to read the couplet as requiring one to forget both the injury received and the good returned, so that the kindness does not become a hidden weapon. The idea is found across traditions: Proverbs and Paul speak of heaping coals of fire on an enemy’s head by feeding him, and the Qur’an promises that repelling evil with what is better can turn an enemy into a close friend. What Valluvar adds is the paradox that the gentlest act is the most effective sanction.

tamil:
அறிவினான் ஆகுவ துண்டோ பிறிதின்நோய்
தந்நோய்போல் போற்றாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Arivinaan aaguvadhu undo piridhin noy
Thannoy pol potraak kadai.
current_meaning: What good is all one’s knowledge if one does not treat another creature’s pain as one’s own and guard it against suffering?
elementary_explanation: You might know lots of facts, like all the planets or every dinosaur. But if your friend falls and scrapes their knee and you don’t care, what good are all those facts? Valluvar says being smart only matters if you feel other people’s hurt like it’s your own.
university_explanation: Valluvar here makes empathy the test of knowledge. Arivu (knowledge, understanding) is asked to justify itself, and the only acceptable answer is that it leads one to regard piridhin noy, the pain of another (piridhu can mean any other being, not only humans), as thannoy, one’s own pain. The verb potru (to guard, protect, cherish) makes the demand active: it is not enough to feel sympathy, one must protect the other from harm as one protects oneself. This anticipates a recurring theme in the Kural that learning without moral application is barren. Comparable ideas appear in the Bhagavad Gita’s claim that true knowledge produces equal vision of all beings, in the Buddha’s reflection that since everyone holds themselves dear no one should harm another, and in the Stoic doctrine of oikeiosis, which asks us to draw the circle of concern outward until strangers are treated as kin.

tamil:
இன்னா எனத்தான் உணர்ந்தவை துன்னாமை
வேண்டும் பிறன்கண் செயல்.
transliteration:
Innaa enaththaan unarndhavai thunnaamai
Vendum piran kan seyal.
current_meaning: Whatever you have learned from your own experience to be painful, you must never do to another person.
elementary_explanation: Remember how much it hurt when someone left you out of a game? Then you already know not to leave anyone else out. This kural says: if something hurt you, don’t do it to others.
university_explanation: This is Valluvar’s clearest statement of the negative Golden Rule, and it is regularly cited alongside Hillel and the Mahabharata in comparative discussions of that principle. The phrase thaan unarndhavai, ‘what one has oneself felt or known,’ grounds the rule in lived experience rather than abstract principle: each person’s own suffering is a textbook of what not to do. Thunnaamai (not approaching, not engaging in) makes the prohibition wide enough to cover even drawing near to such acts. Unlike the positive form (‘do unto others’), the negative form sets a minimum that anyone can meet, and so needs no guesswork about what others want. It closely matches Brihaspati’s summary of dharma in the Mahabharata, Hillel’s one-sentence Torah, and Isocrates’ advice to the Cyprians.

tamil:
எனைத்தானும் எஞ்ஞான்றும் யார்க்கும் மனத்தானாம்
மாணாசெய் யாமை தலை.
transliteration:
Enaiththaanum ennaandrum yaarkkum manaththaanaam
Maanaa seyyaamai thalai.
current_meaning: Never to do any unworthy harm, however small, at any time, to anyone, not even in one’s thoughts, is the highest virtue.
elementary_explanation: Some people only stop themselves from hitting. This kural asks for much more: don’t hurt anyone, not a little bit, not ever, and don’t even plan mean things in your head. That, it says, is the very best kind of goodness.
university_explanation: The couplet universalises the prohibition along every axis at once: degree (enaiththaanum, in any measure however small), time (ennaandrum, at any time), and person (yaarkkum, to anyone). The fourth axis is inward: manaththaan aam, ‘that which arises from the mind,’ which commentators read either as deliberate, knowing harm or as harm committed even in intention. Maanaa means base or ignoble acts. Calling this thalai (the head, the foremost virtue) places total non-harm at the top of the chapter’s ethical hierarchy. Similar demands to extend the prohibition into the inner life appear in Leviticus’ command not to hate one’s brother in the heart, in the First Letter of John, where hatred is equated with murder, and in the Metta Sutta’s wish that no one should even desire harm for another.

tamil:
தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை தானறிவான் என்கொலோ
மன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னா செயல்.
transliteration:
Thannuyirkku innaamai thaan arivaan en kolo
Mannuyirkku innaa seyal.
current_meaning: A person knows well what pain feels like to his own life. Why, then, does he inflict that same pain on other living beings?
elementary_explanation: You know how much a bee sting hurts, because it happened to you. So why would anyone go around stinging others? This kural asks: if you know how pain feels, how can you give it to someone else?
university_explanation: Kural 318 turns the rule of 316 into a question, and the rhetorical form (en kolo, ‘why, then?’) exposes a contradiction in the person who harms. The contrast between thannuyir (one’s own life or self) and mannuyir (the lives that dwell on earth, all living beings) widens the circle beyond humans, in keeping with the Kural’s broad concern for all creatures, developed further in the next chapter on not killing. The argument is essentially one of consistency: whoever knows pain from the inside cannot claim not to know what they are doing when they cause it. Similar appeals to self-knowledge appear in the Gita’s ‘comparison to one’s own self,’ the Dhammapada’s instruction to put oneself in another’s place, and the Torah’s reminder that Israel knows the heart of the stranger because it was once a stranger.

tamil:
பிறர்க்கின்னா முற்பகல் செய்யின் தமக்குஇன்னா
பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும்.
transliteration:
Pirarkku innaa murpagal seyyin thamakku innaa
Pirpagal thaame varum.
current_meaning: If you harm others in the morning, harm will come to you on its own by the afternoon.
elementary_explanation: It’s like throwing a ball hard against a wall: it bounces right back at you. This kural says being mean to someone in the morning means trouble will come bouncing back to you by the afternoon.
university_explanation: This is among the best-known couplets in Tamil, often quoted as a proverb. Its power lies in its compression of time: murpagal (forenoon) and pirpagal (afternoon) shrink the karmic interval, usually imagined across lifetimes, to a single day. The word thaame (of their own accord) makes the return automatic; no avenger or judge is named, and the consequence seems built into the act. The couplet thus combines a moral law with a psychological one, since harm tends to provoke retaliation and hostility quickly. Parallels range from the Mahabharata’s observation that the injured turns round and injures the injurer, to Proverbs’ image of the stone that rolls back on the one who pushes it, to Theseus giving each bandit on the road to Athens the death he dealt to others.

tamil:
நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம் நோய்செய்யார்
நோயின்மை வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Noyellaam noy seydhaar melavaam noy seyyaar
Noyinmai vendu pavar.
current_meaning: All suffering falls upon those who cause suffering; so those who wish to be free of suffering do not cause it to others.
elementary_explanation: If you plant thorns, you will get pricked walking through your own garden. If you never want to get pricked, don’t plant thorns. This kural says: if you want a life without pain, don’t give pain to anyone.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with a verbal tour de force: the word noy (pain, affliction, disease) appears four times in seven words, so that the sound of the couplet enacts its argument that pain circles back to its source. The first line states a law (all affliction settles on those who afflict), and the second draws the practical conclusion for anyone who wants noyinmai, freedom from suffering. The ethics of non-harm is here grounded partly in enlightened self-interest, rounding off a chapter that has moved from the stainless person’s principle (311–312), through empathy (315–318), to consequence (319–320). The idea is widely shared: Hesiod’s warning that the evil plotter harms himself most, the Qur’an’s statement that evil plotting backfires on the plotters, Marcus Aurelius’ remark that the wrongdoer wrongs himself, and the Dhammapada’s assurance that for one who does no evil there is no ill.

tamil:
அறவினை யாதெனின் கொல்லாமை கோறல்
பிறவினை எல்லாந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Aravinai yaadhenin kollaamai koral
Piravinai ellaam tharum.
current_meaning: If you ask what virtuous action is, it is not killing any living being; killing, in turn, brings every other kind of evil deed in its wake.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a row of dominoes. If you knock over the first one, all the others fall too. Valluvar says killing is that first domino: once someone is willing to take a life, every other bad act becomes easy. Not killing keeps the whole row standing.
university_explanation: Valluvar answers the question “what is aram (virtue)?” with a single negative act — kollaamai, abstention from killing — and then gives its mirror image: kōṟal (killing) “yields all other deeds” (piṟavinai), which the classical commentators, including Mu. Varadarasan, read as all non-virtuous deeds. The couplet therefore makes non-killing not merely one virtue among many but the generative root of the moral life, with killing as the root of vice. This places the Kural squarely within the broad śramaṇic and Brahmanical consensus of early-first-millennium India that ahiṃsā is the highest dharma, a position shared by Jain, Buddhist and epic Hindu sources. The structure of the verse — definition followed by its contrary — is typical of Valluvar’s aphoristic logic, compressing an entire ethical theory into seven words.

tamil:
பகுத்துண்டு பல்லுயிர் ஓம்புதல் நூலோர்
தொகுத்தவற்றுள் எல்லாந் தலை.
transliteration:
Pakuththundu palluyir oampudhal nooloar
Thokuththavatrul ellaam thalai.
current_meaning: To share one’s food with others and to protect the many forms of life is the foremost of all the virtues that the learned have gathered together in their books.
elementary_explanation: If you have a lunchbox and a hungry friend, you split your sandwich. If you see a bird with a hurt wing, you help it. Valluvar says that sharing and taking care of every living thing is the number-one rule in all the good books ever written.
university_explanation: The couplet fuses two duties — sharing food (pakuttuṇṭal) and protecting the manifold life of creatures (palluyir ōmputal) — and ranks them as “the head” (talai) of everything the authors of moral treatises (nūlōr) have compiled. Its placement in the chapter on non-killing shows that for Valluvar non-violence is not merely a prohibition but has a positive face: actively sustaining life. The appeal to the collected wisdom of the nūlōr is also a characteristic move, presenting the Kural as a distillation of an entire ethical literature. The pairing of generosity and care for life anticipates modern ethics of care that see nurture, not only abstention from harm, as the core of morality.

tamil:
ஒன்றாக நல்லது கொல்லாமை மற்றதன்
பின்சாரப் பொய்யாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Ondraaka nalladhu kollaamai matradhan
Pinsaarap poiyaamai nandru.
current_meaning: Not killing stands alone as the one peerless good; next after it, and following close behind, comes not lying.
elementary_explanation: Think of a race where first prize is gold and second is silver. Valluvar gives the gold medal to “never kill” and the silver medal to “never lie.” Both are winners, but not hurting any living thing comes first.
university_explanation: Here Valluvar explicitly ranks two virtues he has treated separately: kollaamai (non-killing) is good “as one” (oṉṟāka) — unique and incomparable — and poyyāmai (truthfulness, the subject of chapter 30) is good “following behind it.” This is notable because in chapter 30 he had praised truth in superlative terms; the commentators reconcile the two by saying truth is supreme among virtues of speech, but non-killing is supreme absolutely. The ordering precisely mirrors Patañjali’s list of yamas, where ahiṃsā precedes satya, and the Buddhist precepts, where abstaining from killing is first and false speech fourth. It also contrasts with Gandhi, who, while treating the two as inseparable, made Truth the end and ahimsa the means.

tamil:
நல்லாறு எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும்
கொல்லாமை சூழும் நெறி.
transliteration:
Nallaaru enappaduvadhu yaadhenin yaadhondrum
Kollaamai soozhum neri.
current_meaning: If you ask what is called the good path, it is the way of life that carefully considers how to avoid killing any creature whatsoever.
elementary_explanation: When you walk in a garden, you watch where you step so you don’t squash the ants or crush the flowers. Valluvar says the “good road” in life is exactly that: always looking out so that you don’t hurt even the smallest living thing.
university_explanation: The couplet defines nallāṟu, “the good path,” not by a doctrine or ritual but by a disposition: the neṟi (way of conduct) that “deliberates upon” (cūḻum) not killing “anything at all” (yātoṉṟum). The verb cūḻ suggests active, careful forethought — non-killing is not passive but a vigilant attentiveness in every act. The phrase yātoṉṟum explicitly extends the scope to all living beings, however small, aligning the Kural with the rigorous ahiṃsā of Jain and Buddhist ethics. This conception of ethics as an attentive way of moving through the world anticipates Albert Schweitzer’s “reverence for life.”

tamil:
நிலைஅஞ்சி நீத்தாருள் எல்லாம் கொலைஅஞ்சிக்
கொல்லாமை சூழ்வான் தலை.
transliteration:
Nilaianji neeththaarul ellaam kolaianjik
Kollaamai soozhvaan thalai.
current_meaning: Among all those who, fearing the round of worldly existence, have renounced the world, the foremost is the one who, fearing the sin of killing, carefully keeps to non-killing.
elementary_explanation: Some people give up their toys, their fancy food and their comfy beds to become monks. That’s hard! But Valluvar says the very best of them is the one who is most careful never to hurt a living thing. Being gentle matters more than giving things up.
university_explanation: Valluvar compares two kinds of fear: nilai añci — fear of the “state” of worldly existence and rebirth that drives ascetics to renounce (nīttār) — and kolai añci, fear of the guilt of killing. He declares that among all renunciants, the one moved by the second fear and who deliberates on non-killing is talai, the head. This subordinates the whole apparatus of asceticism to a single ethical commitment, a characteristic Kural move that ranks inner moral conduct over outward religious status. The same move appears in the Mahabharata’s claim that ahimsa is itself the highest penance, and in the Dhammapada’s definition of the true monk as one who has laid down violence toward all beings.

tamil:
கொல்லாமை மேற்கொண் டொழுகுவான் வாழ்நாள்மேல்
செல்லாது உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று.
transliteration:
Kollaamai merkon dozhuguvaan vaazhnaalmel
Sellaadhu uyirunnum kootru.
current_meaning: Death, the devourer of lives, will not advance upon the days of one who has made non-killing the rule of his conduct.
elementary_explanation: In old stories, Death is like a hunter who comes to take people away. Valluvar says that hunter holds back from someone who never hurts any creature — as if even Death respects a person who protects life.
university_explanation: Kūṟṟu, “the one who divides” (Yama, Death), is here personified as “the eater of lives” (uyiruṇṇum). Valluvar claims that it “will not go” (cellātu) against the life-span of one who lives by non-killing. Commentators differ: some read this literally as a promise of long life, others (like Kalaignar) as a poetic image of Death hesitating in awe, and still others spiritually, as freedom from the cycle of rebirth. The idea of karmic reciprocity — sparing life earns life — is explicit in Buddhist teaching on the karmic causes of long and short lives, and has echoes in the biblical promise of prolonged days for sparing the mother bird.

tamil:
தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும் செய்யற்க தான்பிறிது
இன்னுயிர் நீக்கும் வினை.
transliteration:
Thannuyir neeppinum seyyarka thaanpiridhu
Innuyir neekkum vinai.
current_meaning: Even if it would cost you your own life, do not do the deed that takes away the precious life of another being.
elementary_explanation: Suppose a bully says, “Hurt that puppy or I’ll hurt you.” Valluvar says: don’t hurt the puppy, even if you get hurt yourself. The puppy’s life is just as sweet to it as yours is to you.
university_explanation: This is one of the most uncompromising couplets in the Kural: one must not perform “the act that removes another’s sweet life” (piṟitu iṉṉuyir nīkkum viṉai) even if it means losing one’s own. The adjective iṉ (sweet) applied to the other’s life insists on its equal preciousness. Varadarasan explicitly reads it as forbidding killing even to save oneself — a stance close to Jain absolutism and more radical than most legal traditions, which permit self-defence. The Talmud reaches a similar conclusion for the case of being forced to kill an innocent person under threat, reasoning that one cannot know one’s own blood is “redder” than another’s.

tamil:
நன்றாகும் ஆக்கம் பெரிதெனினும் சான்றோர்க்குக்
கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கங் கடை.
transliteration:
Nandraakum aakkam peridheninum saandrorkkuk
Kondraakum aakkam kadai.
current_meaning: Even if the gain it brings is said to be great and good, to the noble-minded any gain that comes through killing is the lowest of things.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone says, “If you trap and kill this bird, you’ll win a huge prize.” A good person says “No, thanks.” Valluvar says a prize that costs a life isn’t a prize at all — it’s the worst kind of win.
university_explanation: Valluvar concedes his opponent’s premise — the prosperity (ākkam) gained may indeed be “great” and even called “good” — and still pronounces it kaṭai, the very lowest, in the eyes of the cāṉṟōr (the noble, perfected ones). Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read the verse as targeting Vedic animal sacrifice (vēḷvi), which promised wealth and heaven through ritual killing; the Kural thus sides with the Jain and Buddhist critique of sacrificial violence. More broadly the couplet rejects consequentialist justifications for killing: no outcome, however beneficial, can redeem the means. The same refusal to let ends justify the taking of life underlies Kant’s formula that persons may never be used merely as means.

tamil:
கொலைவினைய ராகிய மாக்கள் புலைவினையர்
புன்மை தெரிவா ரகத்து.
transliteration:
Kolaivinaiya raagiya maakkal pulaivinaiyar
Punmai therivaa ragaththu.
current_meaning: People who make killing their work are regarded as doers of vile deeds in the minds of those who understand what baseness truly is.
elementary_explanation: Some jobs make you proud, like helping people or growing food. Valluvar says that a job built on killing living things makes wise people think less of you, because they can see how it hardens the heart.
university_explanation: The couplet names the kolaiviṉaiyar, those whose “occupation” (viṉai) is killing, and uses the word mākkaḷ — often reserved for people who have lost human discernment — to describe them. In the minds of those who discern baseness (puṉmai terivār), they are pulaiviṉaiyar, doers of polluted, degraded work. The verse is a moral judgement rather than a caste statement, though the vocabulary of pulai (pollution) reflects the social idiom of its time and should be read critically today. Its underlying insight — that habitual killing corrodes compassion — is shared by the Buddha’s list of wrong livelihoods and by Thomas More’s Utopians, who kept citizens from butchery lest it destroy the feeling of mercy.

tamil:
உயிருடம்பின் நீக்கியா ரென்ப செயிருடம்பின்
செல்லாத்தீ வாழ்க்கை யவர்.
transliteration:
Uyirudambin neekkiyaa renba seyirudambin
Sellaaththee vaazhkkai yavar.
current_meaning: The wise say that those who now live wretched, impoverished lives in diseased bodies are those who once separated life from the bodies of other beings.
elementary_explanation: It’s like planting seeds: if you plant thorns, you get thorns later. Valluvar says that hurting and killing are like planting thorn seeds — sooner or later, sickness and hard times grow back toward the one who planted them.
university_explanation: The final couplet adopts the voice of received wisdom (eṉpa, “they say”): those with diseased bodies (ceyir uṭampu) living a miserable, impoverished life (cellāt tī vāḻkkai) are those who “removed life from bodies” (uyir uṭampiṉ nīkkiyār). All the major commentators read this karmically, as the fruit of killing in a former birth. The couplet closes the chapter by grounding the ethics of non-killing in moral causation; it has parallels in Manu and in the Buddha’s teaching that harming beings leads to sickliness. Modern readers will note that such teaching can be misused to blame the sick and poor — a danger also recognised within other traditions, as when Jesus rejects the idea that a man’s blindness was caused by sin (John 9:3).

tamil:
நில்லாத வற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்
புல்லறி வாண்மை கடை.
transliteration:
Nillaadha vatrai nilaiyina endru unarum
Pullarivu aanmai kadai.
current_meaning: To take things that cannot last and believe they are permanent is the lowest kind of foolishness.
elementary_explanation: Imagine building a sandcastle and believing it will stay on the beach forever, even though the waves always come. This kural says that treating things that will surely change or go away as if they will last forever is the silliest mistake a person can make.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter on impermanence not with a description of transience but with an epistemic judgement: the root error is a false cognition, mistaking the non-abiding (nillaadhavai) for the abiding (nilaiyina). The phrase “pullarivaanmai” (petty-mindedness, a paltry intelligence that presumes itself competent) frames the problem as a defect of understanding rather than of morals, and “kadai” (the lowest, the most base) ranks it at the bottom of human conditions. Commentators from Parimelazhagar onward read the chapter as the doorway of the renunciate section (thuravaraviyal), since recognising impermanence (nilaiyaamai) is what loosens attachment and makes renunciation (the next chapter, thuravu) intelligible. The idea sits close to the Buddhist and Jain analysis of avidya/moha, where suffering follows from treating the impermanent as permanent, and to the Stoic insistence that disturbance comes from our judgements about things rather than from the things themselves.

tamil:
கூத்தாட்டு அவைக்குழாத் தற்றே பெருஞ்செல்வம்
போக்கும் அதுவிளிந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Koothaattu avaikkuzhaath thatre perunjelvam
Pokkum adhu vilindhatru.
current_meaning: Great wealth gathers the way a crowd gathers at a dance performance, and it leaves the way that crowd scatters when the show is over.
elementary_explanation: Think of people crowding in to watch a street show. When the show ends, everyone walks away at once and the place is empty. This kural says money is like that crowd: it comes in bit by bit, and it can leave all at once.
university_explanation: Valluvar builds the couplet on a single theatrical simile with two halves: the assembling of an audience (koothaattu avaik kuzhaam) and its dispersal when the performance ends (adhu vilindhatru). Commentators note the asymmetry the image implies: an audience trickles in gradually but leaves together, just as wealth is accumulated slowly and can vanish in a single reversal. The theatre is also suggestive, since the crowd was never attached to the patron but to the spectacle, much as wealth is never truly bound to its holder. The kural therefore relocates wealth from the category of possession to that of event, something that happens around a person for a time. Comparable ideas appear in the Greek theme of the reversal of fortune (Solon and Croesus) and in the Stoic teaching that external goods are on loan.

tamil:
அற்கா இயல்பிற்றுச் செல்வம் அதுபெற்றால்
அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்.
transliteration:
Arkaa iyalbitruch selvam adhu petraal
Arkupa aange seyal.
current_meaning: Wealth is by nature unstable; so when you have it, use it at once to do the good deeds that last.
elementary_explanation: If you are given ice cream on a hot day, you should share it right away before it melts. This kural says money is like that ice cream: it won't stay, so use it for good things now, while you still have it.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a deliberate play between “arkaa” (that which does not stay) and “arkupa” (things that do stay, that is, enduring deeds), both drawn from the verb ‘ar’, to abide. Valluvar thus converts a descriptive claim about wealth into an imperative: since wealth is non-abiding, use it for what abides, and do so “aange” (then and there, at once). Commentators identify the enduring deeds with the householder virtues discussed earlier in the work, such as hospitality, charity and helpfulness (oppuravu). The logic is an ethical economics: a perishable asset should be exchanged immediately for an imperishable one before it spoils. The same move, turning transient riches into lasting merit, appears in the Gospel's ‘treasures in heaven’, the Quran's ‘enduring good deeds’, and Bhartrhari's teaching that wealth has only three destinies.

tamil:
நாளென ஒன்றுபோற் காட்டி உயிர்ஈரும்
வாளது உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Naal ena ondru pol kaatti uyir eerum
Vaal adhu unarvaar perin.
current_meaning: The day presents itself as a simple unit of time, but to those who understand, it is really a saw that cuts away at life.
elementary_explanation: Each day feels like just another day: you wake up, play, and sleep. But every day that passes is one less day you have left, like a saw slowly cutting through a log. This kural says wise people notice this.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on an unmasking: “naal” (the day) displays itself (kaatti) as a neutral thing, an ordinary measure of time, but its real nature is a “vaal” (blade, commonly understood as a saw) that “eerum” (cleaves, saws through) life. The verb eer suggests the slow back-and-forth of a saw rather than a single cut, so life is shown being worn away in daily strokes. The conditional “unarvaarp perin” (if one finds those who understand) implies that such people are rare; most take the passing day at face value. Philosophically the kural anticipates Seneca's remark that we die daily and the Psalmist's prayer to ‘number our days’: time is not a container in which life takes place, but the very process by which life is used up.

tamil:
நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன் நல்வினை
மேற்சென்று செய்யப் படும்.
transliteration:
Naachchetru vikkul mel vaaraamun nalvinai
Mersendru seyyap padum.
current_meaning: Before the tongue is stilled and the death rattle rises in the throat, hurry to do good deeds.
elementary_explanation: If you want to say sorry or help someone, don't wait for ‘someday’, because someday might not come. This kural says do your good deeds now, while you still can talk and act.
university_explanation: Valluvar gives the chapter's abstract point a stark physical image: “naa chetru” (the tongue locked or stilled) and “vikkul mel vaaraa mun” (before the hiccup, the death rattle, rises), which are the classical signs of the last moments of life. The imperative “mersendru” (going forward, pressing ahead) carries the sense of taking the initiative and not waiting for circumstances. The image of a silenced tongue also implies that at the end one cannot even speak one's intentions, let alone carry them out. The kural thus moves from recognising impermanence to acting urgently, an ethic of timeliness found in Rabbi Eliezer's ‘repent one day before your death’, the Quran's warning against wishing for a reprieve at death, and Marcus Aurelius' ‘while it is in thy power, be good’.

tamil:
நெருநல் உளனொருவன் இன்றில்லை என்னும்
பெருமை உடைத்துஇவ் வுலகு.
transliteration:
Nerunal ulan oruvan indru illai ennum
Perumai udaiththu ivvulagu.
current_meaning: This world has the ‘greatness’ of being a place where someone who was here yesterday is gone today.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes we hear, ‘I just saw him yesterday, and now he's gone.’ This kural says that is simply how the world works: people can be here one day and gone the next.
university_explanation: The couplet is famous for its irony. “Perumai” (greatness, glory) is normally praise, but Valluvar awards it to the world for the most unsettling of distinctions, that a man alive “nerunal” (yesterday) is not there “indru” (today). Commentators such as the thirukkural-thamizh gloss explicitly read perumai here as a mocking word for the world's instability. The unit of time is only a single day, which heightens the sense of suddenness. The world's one reliable ‘achievement’ is the constant disappearance of its inhabitants. The observation echoes the Yaksha's question in the Mahabharata about the wonder of human denial of death, and Marcus Aurelius' remark about yesterday's mucus becoming tomorrow's ashes.

tamil:
ஒருபொழுதும் வாழ்வது அறியார் கருதுப
கோடியும் அல்ல பல.
transliteration:
Oru pozhudhum vaazhvadhu ariyaar karudhupa
Kodiyum alla pala.
current_meaning: People who cannot know whether they will live even one more moment still make plans beyond counting, more than ten million.
elementary_explanation: Someone might plan what they'll do next week, next year, and in ten years, even though nobody knows for sure what will happen tomorrow. This kural gently laughs at how many plans we make when we can't even be sure of the next hour.
university_explanation: The couplet's force comes from the mismatch of scale: “oru pozhudhu” (a single moment or watch of the day) against “kodiyum alla pala” (not a crore, i.e. ten million, but more). People who cannot guarantee a single stretch of time still carry countless projects, desires and calculations. Commentators note the progression within the chapter from “yesterday/today” (336) to an even smaller unit, “one moment” (337), tightening the frame of uncertainty. The critique is not of planning as such but of a mind that lives in imagined futures while forgetting its own fragility. The Gita's portrait of the deluded man counting his gains ‘today’ and ‘tomorrow’, Jesus' parable of the rich fool, and Aeschylus' ‘blind hopes’ all diagnose the same condition.

tamil:
குடம்பை தனித்துஒழியப் புள்பறந் தற்றே
உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு.
transliteration:
Kudambai thaniththu ozhiyap pul parandhatre
Udambodu uyiridai natpu.
current_meaning: The bond between body and soul is like that of a bird and the egg (or nest) it leaves behind, empty and alone, when it flies away.
elementary_explanation: A baby bird grows inside an egg, but one day it breaks out and flies off, leaving the empty shell behind. This kural says our life and our body are like that: one day life flies off, and the body is left behind like the shell.
university_explanation: The meaning turns on the word “kudambai”, which Parimelazhagar and many commentators gloss as ‘egg’ (so the chick breaks out and leaves the shell), while others read it as ‘nest’ (so a grown bird abandons its home); both readings agree that the container is left “thaniththu ozhiya” (abandoned, alone). Calling the relationship “natpu” (friendship) is pointed, since it is a friendship of convenience that ends the moment the occupant departs. The egg reading adds the idea that the body was the soul's place of formation, not its permanent home, which prepares for kural 340. The image of soul and body as distinct, one of them leaving the other, parallels the Gita's worn-out garments, Ecclesiastes' spirit returning to God, and Plato's definition of death in the Phaedo as the separation of soul from body.

tamil:
உறங்கு வதுபோலுஞ் சாக்காடு உறங்கி
விழிப்பது போலும் பிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Urangu vadhu polum saakkaadu urangi
Vizhippadhu polum pirappu.
current_meaning: Death is like falling asleep, and birth is like waking up after sleep.
elementary_explanation: Every night you fall asleep, and every morning you wake up again. This kural says dying is like falling asleep, and being born is like waking up.
university_explanation: The couplet is the chapter's most compressed statement: “saakkaadu” (death) is like “uranguvadhu” (sleeping), and “pirappu” (birth) is like “urangi vizhippadhu” (waking after sleep). Most traditional commentators read it within the Indian framework of rebirth: death and birth follow one another as naturally as sleep and waking, so the cycle is familiar rather than terrifying, and the real goal is to escape it (veedu). Some modern readers, including Kalaignar's gloss, take a more secular line, stressing that death is a sleep from which one does not wake. The analogy is found across traditions: the Greek twins Hypnos and Thanatos, Socrates' ‘dreamless sleep’, the biblical ‘those who sleep in the dust’ shall awake, and the Quran's teaching that God takes souls both in death and in sleep.

tamil:
புக்கில் அமைந்தின்று கொல்லோ உடம்பினுள்
துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Pukkil amaindhindru kollo udambinul
Thuchchil irundha uyirkku.
current_meaning: It seems that the soul, which only lodges for a while in a corner of the body, has not yet found a permanent home of its own.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a traveller who keeps staying in borrowed rooms, moving from one to the next, never having a house of their own. This kural says the soul is like that traveller: the body is only a temporary room, and it is still looking for its true home.
university_explanation: Valluvar closes the chapter with a question rather than a statement. “Pukkil” (a settled dwelling, a home one enters to stay) is contrasted with “thuchchil” (a temporary lodging, a borrowed corner), and the particle “kollo” (is it perhaps that...?) gives the line a tone of wondering. The soul is pictured as a tenant in a rented corner of the body, which explains why it keeps moving from body to body: it has not yet reached its true home, which traditional commentators identify with veedu (liberation). The chapter thus moves from wealth (332-333), to time (334-337), to the body (338-339), and finally to the homelessness of the soul, handing on to the next chapter on renunciation. Parallels include the Gita's ‘transient world’ from which liberated souls do not return, Paul's ‘earthly house of this tabernacle’, the hadith of being a ‘stranger or traveller’, and Marcus Aurelius' ‘stranger's sojourn’.

tamil:
யாதனின் யாதனின் நீங்கியான் நோதல்
அதனின் அதனின் இலன்.
transliteration:
Yaadhanin yaadhanin neengiyaan nodhal
Adhanin adhanin ilan.
current_meaning: Whatever thing a person has freed himself from — whatever it may be — from that very thing he suffers no more pain.
elementary_explanation: If you stop caring about keeping a certain toy, you won't cry when it breaks. This kural says every single thing you stop clinging to is one less thing that can make you sad.
university_explanation: The doubled pronouns (yaadhanin yaadhanin … adhanin adhanin, “from whatever, whatever … from that, that”) set up an exact one-to-one ledger: each object released cancels the suffering tied to that particular object. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as the gradualist justification for renunciation — one need not abandon everything at once to begin reaping relief, since each detachment pays its own dividend; Karunanidhi likewise glosses it as “whichever single attachment one gives up.” The chapter therefore opens not with an ascetic command but with a near-empirical observation about the mechanics of grief: pain travels along the line of attachment. The same causal claim underlies the Buddhist analysis of suffering as arising from clinging (upādāna) and the Stoic insistence that distress comes from our relation to externals rather than from the externals themselves.

tamil:
வேண்டின்உண் டாகத் துறக்க துறந்தபின்
ஈண்டுஇயற் பால பல.
transliteration:
Vendin undaagath thurakka thurandhapin
Eendu iyarpaala pala.
current_meaning: If you want lasting good, renounce while you still have things to renounce; once you have renounced, many joys become available even here in this life.
elementary_explanation: Taking a heavy backpack off before a long hike isn't losing anything — it's how you get to enjoy the walk. This kural says give things up while you still have them, and you'll find lots of happiness right away.
university_explanation: The phrase undaaga (“while [they] exist”) is read by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan as a timing instruction: renounce while wealth, strength and opportunity are still in hand, not after they have already slipped away — giving up what one no longer has is not renunciation at all. The second line's eendu (“here”, in this world) is striking: Valluvar promises not only a post-mortem reward but many present goods (iyarpaala pala), countering the caricature of renunciation as pure deprivation. This anticipates the famous Upanishadic paradox that one enjoys by relinquishing. Placed after the Kural's earlier praise of the householder (ch. 5, Ilvaazhkai), the couplet presents thuravu as a voluntary, later-chosen stage rather than a universal command.

tamil:
அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை விடல்வேண்டும்
வேண்டிய வெல்லாம் ஒருங்கு.
transliteration:
Adalvendum aindhan pulaththai vidalvendum
Vendiya vellaam orungu.
current_meaning: One must subdue the five senses and, at the same time, give up together everything those senses crave.
elementary_explanation: Imagine five puppies each pulling you toward a different treat. You need to hold all five leashes AND put all the treats away. This kural says control all five senses and let go of everything they want, all at once.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on two parallel imperatives (adalvendum … vidalvendum, “must conquer … must abandon”): conquest of the five sense-fields (aindhan pulam — sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch) and the simultaneous relinquishing of all that they desire. The final word orungu (“together, all at once”) is decisive; Parimelazhagar stresses that a partial abandonment leaves a foothold from which desire regrows. Pairing inner control with outer relinquishment mirrors the Indic scheme of indriya-nigraha and tyaga, and recalls Kural 6's praise of the one who has quenched the five sense-gates. Across traditions the senses appear as the doorways through which the world lays claim to the self — the Gita's tortoise, Plato's unruly horse, Odysseus's wax-stopped crew.

tamil:
இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கொன்று இன்மை உடைமை
மயலாகும் மற்றும் பெயர்த்து.
transliteration:
Iyalbaagum nonbirkondru inmai udaimai
Mayalaagum matrum peyarththu.
current_meaning: Owning nothing at all is the natural condition of true austerity; possessing even one thing turns a person back into the very delusion he had left behind.
elementary_explanation: If you are trying to stop eating sweets, keeping 'just one piece' in your pocket makes it very hard to stop thinking about sweets. This kural says someone who has given things up should keep nothing, because even one thing can pull them back.
university_explanation: Inmai (having nothing) is called the iyalbu — the natural, defining character — of nonbu (austerity, tapas). The second line's peyarththu (“turning back, reversing”) suggests that possession does not merely distract but undoes progress, returning the renunciant to mayal, bewilderment; Karunanidhi glosses that even one attachment multiplies into many. This is a stricter standard than Kural 341's gradualism, and it applies specifically to one who has already taken up the ascetic life. Comparable rules shaped the Buddhist monk's short list of requisites, the Jain ideal of aparigraha, and the apostolic mission charge in Matthew 10; the Cynic Diogenes made the same point theatrically.

tamil:
மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல் பிறப்பறுக்கல்
உற்றார்க்கு உடம்பும் மிகை.
transliteration:
Matrum thodarppaadu evankol pirapparukkal
Utraarkku udambum migai.
current_meaning: For those who are striving to end the cycle of birth, even the body is one thing too many — so why take on any further ties?
elementary_explanation: If you are trying to swim across a river, even your shoes feel heavy. Why would you carry a suitcase too? This kural says someone trying to be truly free finds even their own body a load, so they shouldn't add extra burdens.
university_explanation: The couplet argues a fortiori: if even the body — the one attachment that cannot simply be discarded — is migai (excess, surplus) to someone who has set out to cut off births (pirappu arukkal), then every additional bond (thodarppaadu) is indefensible. Parimelazhagar notes that the body is retained only as the instrument through which austerity is practised, not valued for its own sake. The verse does not counsel harming the body; it relocates the body from 'self' to 'tool'. The idea resonates with Plato's Phaedo, where philosophy is a rehearsal for the soul's release from the body, with Paul's groaning 'in this tabernacle', and with the Buddha's house-builder verse, in which the body is the house craving keeps rebuilding.

tamil:
யானென தென்னுஞ் செருக்கறுப்பான் வானோர்க்
குயர்ந்த உலகம் புகும்.
transliteration:
Yaanenadhu ennum serukkaruppaan vaanork
kuyarndha ulagam pugum.
current_meaning: One who cuts away the pride that says “I” and “mine” will enter a world higher even than the world of the gods.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a kid who stops shouting 'Mine! Mine!' about every toy and stops acting like everything is about them. This kural says a person who drops 'me' and 'mine' reaches a place even better than heaven.
university_explanation: Yaan (“I”) and enadhu (“mine”) are the Tamil counterparts of ahankara and mamakara; Parimelazhagar glosses them as mistaking the body for the self and taking unconnected things as one's own, and calls this pairing serukku — pride or delusion. The reward, vaanorkku uyarndha ulagam (“a world higher than the gods'”), is read by traditional commentators as liberation (veedu), which lies beyond even the heavens, themselves impermanent. Karunanidhi, consistent with his rationalist reading, renders it instead as a renown surpassing heaven's. The couplet thus makes ego itself, not property, the root to be severed — property is simply 'mine' extended outward. The parallel with Gita 2.71 (nirmamo nirahankarah, 'without mine, without ego') is almost verbatim.

tamil:
பற்றி விடாஅ இடும்பைகள் பற்றினைப்
பற்றி விடாஅ தவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Patri vidaaa idumbaigal patrinaip
Patri vidaaa thavarkku.
current_meaning: Sorrows seize and never let go of those who seize their attachments and will not let them go.
elementary_explanation: If you grab a cactus and refuse to let go, it keeps hurting you. This kural says when you hang on tightly to things, troubles hang on tightly to you.
university_explanation: One of the Kural's most celebrated pieces of wordplay: the phrase patri vidaaa (“seizing, not releasing”) appears twice, first describing sorrows (idumbaigal) and then describing people who hold on to patru (attachment). The mirror structure enacts the moral — the grip we exert is the grip exerted upon us. Mu. Varadarasan specifies the attachments as the twofold 'I' and 'mine' of the previous couplet, making this verse the causal explanation of Kural 346. The same self-reinforcing loop is analysed in Buddhist accounts of craving, in the Gita's chain from dwelling on objects to attachment to desire, and in Spinoza's description of human bondage to the passions.

tamil:
தலைப்பட்டார் தீரத் துறந்தார் மயங்கி
வலைப்பட்டார் மற்றை யவர்.
transliteration:
Thalaippattaar theerath thurandhaar mayangi
Valaippattaar matrai yavar.
current_meaning: Those who have renounced completely have reached the highest goal; all the others, bewildered, are caught in the net.
elementary_explanation: A fish that swims completely clear of the net stays free, but a fish that stays near it 'just a little' gets caught. This kural says people who give up everything are truly free, while the rest get tangled up.
university_explanation: Theera (“wholly, to the very end”) is the key word: Valluvar contrasts complete renunciants, who have thalaippattaar — 'reached the head', attained the goal — with the rest, who, bewildered (mayangi), are valaippattaar, 'netted'. The rhyming pair thalaippattaar/valaippattaar sharpens the stark binary. Commentators differ over the net: Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as the net of repeated births, Mu. Varadarasan and Karunanidhi as the net of ignorance. The couplet refuses any comfortable middle position — a half-renunciation still counts as capture — in line with Luke 9:62's warning against looking back from the plough and the Gita's 'mesh of delusion'.

tamil:
பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும் மற்று
நிலையாமை காணப் படும்.
transliteration:
Patratra kanne pirapparukkum matru
Nilaiyaamai kaanap padum.
current_meaning: At the very moment attachment ceases, the cycle of birth is cut; otherwise, instability — the endless round of coming and going — is what will be seen.
elementary_explanation: A spinning top keeps going as long as you keep flicking it; stop flicking, and it finally rests. This kural says once you stop clinging, the cycle of being born again and again stops — and if you don't, everything keeps wobbling and changing.
university_explanation: Kanne (“at that very point”) stresses immediacy: liberation coincides with the cessation of patru rather than following it as a later reward. The second line is read in two ways. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan take matru as 'otherwise': without detachment, instability — the alternation of births and deaths — will be seen. Puliyur Kesikan reads it as 'moreover': with detachment, the impermanence of the world is then clearly seen. Either way the couplet binds this chapter to the preceding one, Nilaiyaamai (Impermanence, ch. 34). The claim that the end of desire is the end of rebirth is shared almost word for word by the Katha Upanishad and the Dhammapada, and appears inverted in the Orphic hope of escaping the 'wheel'.

tamil:
பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை அப்பற்றைப்
பற்றுக பற்று விடற்கு.
transliteration:
Patruga patratraan patrinai appatraip
Patruga patru vidarku.
current_meaning: Hold fast to the One who is free of all attachment; hold fast to that attachment alone, so that you can let go of every other.
elementary_explanation: When you're learning to swim, you hold on to the edge of the pool so you can stop being scared of the water. This kural says hold on to God — the one who clings to nothing — so you can let go of everything else.
university_explanation: The chapter's closing couplet repeats forms of patru (“attachment, clinging”) six times, a virtuoso climax. It resolves a paradox the chapter has built up: desire cannot simply be willed away, so Valluvar prescribes a single counter-attachment — to patratraan, 'the One without attachment', whom Parimelazhagar and most commentators identify as God, whose feet are to be held — as the instrument for dropping all other attachments. Karunanidhi, in keeping with his secular reading, takes patratraan to mean any truly detached person, making the verse a counsel to cling to the company of the detached. The strategy of replacing a lower attachment with a higher one parallels the Gita's 'higher taste', while the Buddha's raft simile adds the caution that even the means is finally to be let go.

tamil:
பொருளல்ல வற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும்
மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Porulalla vatraip porulendru unarum
Marulaanaam maanaap pirappu.
current_meaning: Taking things that are not real to be the real thing is a delusion, and it is from this delusion that a birth without dignity arises: the endless round of lowly rebirths.
elementary_explanation: Imagine chasing a shiny puddle on a hot road, sure it’s water, when it’s only a mirage. You’d run and run, get more and more thirsty, and never drink. This kural says that when we treat things that don’t last as if they were the real treasure, we keep chasing mirages again and again, life after life.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with a diagnosis rather than a prescription: the root of bondage is marul (delusion, confusion), specifically the cognitive error of taking porul-alladhu (what is not the real) for porul (the real). Commentators such as Parimelazhagar read maanaa-p-pirappu (‘inglorious birth’) as the whole cycle of transmigration, which turns the couplet into an epistemological account of samsara: rebirth is caused less by particular sins than by misperception. This closely matches the Advaita Vedanta analysis of adhyasa (superimposition, the classic rope mistaken for a snake) and the Buddhist teaching that avijja (ignorance) is the first link of dependent origination. Because the Tamil ‘porul’ is richly ambiguous (thing, wealth, meaning, reality), the couplet also carries an ethical undertone: whoever treats wealth and possessions as the ultimate ‘thing’ has mistaken the counterfeit for the coin.

tamil:
இருள்நீங்கி இன்பம் பயக்கும் மருள்நீங்கி
மாசறு காட்சி யவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Irulneengi inbam payakkum marulneengi
Maasaru kaatchi yavarkku.
current_meaning: For those who have left delusion behind and gained a clear, flawless vision of the truth, that vision drives away the darkness and brings true bliss.
elementary_explanation: When you switch on the light in a dark room, the scary shape in the corner turns out to be just a coat on a chair, and suddenly you feel safe and happy. People who see the truth clearly are like that: the light of truth chases away the darkness and fear, and joy comes in.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a matched pair: irul neengi (darkness departs) and marul neengi (delusion departs). When inner confusion (marul) is removed, outer darkness (irul, which commentators gloss as the darkness of hell or of future births) also lifts. The key phrase maasaru kaatchi, ‘stainless seeing’, frames liberation as a kind of vision (compare the Sanskrit darshana) rather than mere intellectual agreement, and Parimelazhagar takes the resulting inbam (bliss) as the bliss of release (veedu). The light/darkness metaphor for knowledge and ignorance is shared with the Upanishads (tamaso ma jyotir gamaya), with the Buddha’s first sermon (‘illumination arose’), and with Plato’s ascent from the cave. What stands out in Valluvar is the ethical precondition built into the seeing itself: the vision must be free of stain (maasu).

tamil:
ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு வையத்தின்
வானம் நணிய துடைத்து.
transliteration:
Aiyaththin neengith thelindhaarkku vaiyaththin
Vaanam naniya thudaiththu.
current_meaning: For those who have moved beyond doubt and reached clear certainty, heaven is nearer than the very earth they stand on.
elementary_explanation: When you’re not sure which path leads home, even a short walk feels long and scary. But once you know the way for certain, home feels close. This kural says that people who have cleared away all doubt about what is true feel heaven is closer to them than the ground under their feet.
university_explanation: Aiyam (doubt) is here a technical term: Indian epistemology treats samshaya (doubt) as one of the defects of cognition that block liberation, alongside viparyaya (error), which Kural 351 addressed. Thelivu (clarity, settled understanding) is the positive term, and Valluvar’s hyperbole (vaanam naniyadhu, ‘the sky/heaven is nearer’) turns ordinary spatial logic upside down: the earth we stand on becomes the distant, precarious thing, while the spiritual goal becomes immediate. Commentators take vaanam as the higher world or liberation (veedu). The inversion echoes the Gita’s warning that the doubting soul finds happiness neither here nor hereafter, and the Mundaka Upanishad’s ‘all doubts are solved’ when the Real is seen. Comparative readers may also note Deuteronomy’s insistence that the divine word is ‘not in heaven’ but ‘very nigh unto thee’, a similar collapsing of distance, though grounded in revelation rather than insight.

tamil:
ஐயுணர்வு எய்தியக் கண்ணும் பயமின்றே
மெய்யுணர்வு இல்லா தவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Aiyunarvu eydhiyak kannum payamindre
Meyyunarvu illaa thavarkku.
current_meaning: Even if someone has fully mastered all that the five senses can know, it brings no real benefit if they lack true knowledge of reality.
elementary_explanation: A person could have perfect eyes, sharp ears and a great nose, and still walk right past a treasure because they don’t know what it is. This kural says the five senses are like a camera: very useful, but you need a wise mind to understand what the pictures really mean.
university_explanation: Aiyunarvu, ‘five-fold awareness’, has two classical readings, both preserved in the commentary tradition. Mu. Varadarasanar and others take it as the complete knowledge gathered through the five senses, while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as the ascetic’s mastery or restraint of the five senses. Either way the claim is striking: neither sensory knowledge nor sensory discipline is enough without meyyunarvu, knowledge of the real. The second reading turns the couplet into a pointed warning to renunciants (the chapter sits in the Thuravaraviyal, the section on the ascetic life) that austerity without insight is barren. Philosophically it anticipates the argument of Plato’s Theaetetus that knowledge cannot simply be perception, and it parallels Heraclitus’s remark that eyes and ears are bad witnesses for souls that cannot interpret them.

tamil:
எப்பொருள் எத்தன்மைத் தாயினும் அப்பொருள்
மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு.
transliteration:
Epporul eththanmaith thaayinum apporul
Meypporul kaanpadhu arivu.
current_meaning: Whatever a thing may be, and however it may appear, wisdom is seeing the true reality within that thing.
elementary_explanation: Two chocolates can look exactly the same, but one might have caramel inside and the other a nut. You only know by looking inside. This kural says a wise person doesn’t stop at how things look on the outside but finds out what they really are.
university_explanation: This is the chapter’s most quoted couplet, and it works as a definition: arivu (wisdom) is meypporul kaanpadhu, ‘seeing the true thing’ in every porul, whatever its apparent nature (eththanmaith thaayinum). The chain of repetitions (epporul, apporul, meypporul) performs the act it describes, peeling ‘thing’ back to ‘true thing’. Mu. Varadarasanar’s gloss makes the point explicit: one must not be dazzled by how a thing appears but know its real nature. Modern readers often extend it to critical thinking in general, meaning not being taken in by surface, reputation, or rhetoric. The ideal is close to the Buddhist yathabhuta-ñanadassana (‘knowing and seeing things as they really are’) and to the Greek project, from Heraclitus to Plato, of distinguishing a thing’s real nature (phusis) from how it seems (doxa).

tamil:
கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார் தலைப்படுவர்
மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி.
transliteration:
Katreendu meypporul kandaar thalaippaduvar
Matreendu vaaraa neri.
current_meaning: Those who have learned, and here in this very life have seen the True Reality, set out on the path that never returns here again.
elementary_explanation: When you finally solve a really hard maze, you don’t have to go back into it: you’ve found the way out. This kural says that people who learn deeply and truly understand what is real find the way out of the maze of being born again and again.
university_explanation: Two emphases distinguish this couplet: kattru (having learned) and eendu (here, in this very life). Valluvar insists that realization must happen within embodied existence, a ‘liberation while living’ close to the Vedantic jivanmukti and to the Buddhist arahant who knows ‘this is the last birth’. Learning is the necessary first step, but the verb is kandaar (they saw), not merely ‘they studied’: scholarship must end in direct seeing, and Solomon Pappaiah’s gloss stresses learning from the great as the start of that process. Vaaraa neri, ‘the path of no return’, closely echoes the Gita’s ‘one who reaches it never returns’. The formula reaches across traditions: Revelation’s ‘he shall go no more out’ and the Orphic initiate’s escape from the ‘circle’ of births voice the same idea of a final exit.

tamil:
ஓர்த்துள்ளம் உள்ளது உணரின் ஒருதலையாப்
பேர்த்துள்ள வேண்டா பிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Orththullam ulladhu unarin orudhalaiyaap
Perththulla vendaa pirappu.
current_meaning: If the mind has carefully examined and firmly grasped That Which Truly Is, there is no need to think of being born again.
elementary_explanation: Once you truly understand that the monster under the bed was only a shadow, you don’t have to be scared of it again tomorrow night. This kural says that once your mind really and firmly understands what is real, you don’t have to worry about coming back to be born again.
university_explanation: Ulladhu, literally ‘that which is’, is one of the most philosophically loaded words in the chapter. It corresponds to the Sanskrit sat (Being) and later gave its name to Ramana Maharshi’s Tamil work Ulladhu Narpadhu (‘Forty Verses on That Which Is’). Orththu (having reflected or investigated) and oru-thalaiyaa (with complete, one-pointed certainty) spell out the method: truth is reached by sustained inquiry until conviction is total. Traditional glosses (Solomon Pappaiah speaks of holding fully in mind ‘what was heard from the great’) connect this to the Vedantic sequence of hearing, reflection and contemplation (shravana, manana, nididhyasana). The language of ‘what is’ invites comparison with Parmenides, for whom Being is ‘uncreated and indestructible’, and with Maimonides, for whom knowing the Primary Being is ‘the foundation of all foundations’. Valluvar’s distinctive claim is soteriological: to grasp Being is to end becoming.

tamil:
பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை நீங்கச் சிறப்பென்னும்
செம்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு.
transliteration:
Pirappennum pedhaimai neengach sirappennum
Semporul kaanpadhu arivu.
current_meaning: True wisdom is seeing the perfect Truth, called the Supreme Good, so that the folly called ‘birth’ is removed.
elementary_explanation: Imagine being stuck on a merry-go-round that never stops because you forgot there’s an exit. The moment you notice the exit sign, you can step off. This kural says being born again and again is like forgetting the exit, and seeing what is truly real is the exit sign.
university_explanation: The couplet makes a bold equation: pirappu ennum pedhaimai, ‘the folly called birth’. Birth is not only caused by ignorance (as in 351); it is itself named a form of ignorance. Against it stands sirappu ennum semporul, ‘the perfect Truth called excellence’, which commentators read as the Supreme Being or the state of release (Mu. Varadarasanar glosses sirappu as mukti). Semporul (‘the fine, perfect substance’) is the same term used in 359 for the support of all things. Buddhism offers the closest structural parallel: in dependent origination, ignorance (avijja) is the first condition and rebirth (jati) the eleventh, so the fading of ignorance ends birth. Hindu parallels such as Gita 4.9 make knowledge of the divine the reason one ‘does not take birth again’, while John’s ‘the truth shall make you free’ expresses liberation through knowing within a linear rather than cyclical cosmology.

tamil:
சார்புணர்ந்து சார்பு கெடஒழுகின் மற்றழித்துச்
சார்தரா சார்தரு நோய்.
transliteration:
Saarbunarndhu saarbu keda ozhukin matrazhiththuch
Saardharaa saardharu noi.
current_meaning: Whoever understands the true Support of all things, and lives so that every lesser attachment falls away, will find that the sorrows that would have clung to them, destroying their efforts, cling no more.
elementary_explanation: If you’re holding a hundred balloons, the wind can drag you anywhere. But if you let go of them and hold on to one strong railing, you stay safe. This kural says: know what is truly worth holding on to, let the other things go, and troubles can’t grab hold of you.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a remarkable pun: the root saar- (‘to lean on, cling to, attach’) appears four times: saarbu unarndhu (knowing the true support), saarbu keda (so that attachments perish), saardharaa (will not cling) and saardharu noi (the afflictions that would cling). Commentators read the first saarbu as the Supreme Truth (semporul), the support of all things, and the second as worldly attachment (pattru). The wordplay thus contrasts one legitimate ‘leaning’ with many illegitimate ones. The logic, that attachment is the channel through which suffering ‘attaches’, is shared with Buddhist teaching on upadana (grasping) and with the Gita’s call to cut the world-tree ‘with the weapon of detachment’ while taking refuge in its root. Islam’s divine name as-Samad, the One on whom all depend, offers an especially close lexical parallel to the first saarbu.

tamil:
காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் இவ்மூன்றன்
நாமம் கெடக்கெடும் நோய்.
transliteration:
Kaamam vekuli mayakkam ivmoondran
Naamam kedakkedum noi.
current_meaning: When desire, anger and delusion (these three) are destroyed so completely that even their names are gone, the suffering they cause is destroyed too.
elementary_explanation: Weeds keep coming back if you only snip off the tops. You have to pull them out by the roots so nothing is left. This kural says greed, anger and confusion are like three weeds: pull them out so completely that even their names are forgotten, and the trouble they cause disappears.
university_explanation: The chapter closes by naming a triad: kaamam, vekuli, mayakkam (desire, anger, delusion). Its correspondence with the Buddhist ‘three roots’ or ‘three poisons’ (raga, dosa, moha: greed, hatred, delusion) is nearly exact, and it overlaps substantially with the Gita’s ‘three gates of hell’ (lust, anger, greed).
