Valluvar’s hyperbole, that the very names must perish (naamam keda), insists on eradication rather than suppression: not even the latent tendency or memory may remain. Because the chapter began with delusion (marul) as the cause of birth, ending with mayakkam as the third root closes the argument in a ring. True knowledge removes the delusion that fuels desire and anger, and with all three gone, the ‘disease’ (noi) of suffering and rebirth ends.

tamil:
அவாஎன்ப எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து.
transliteration:
Avaa enba ellaa uyirkkum egnaandrum
Thavaaap pirappeenum viththu.
current_meaning: The wise say that desire is the seed which, for every living being and at every time, unfailingly produces birth after birth.
elementary_explanation: A seed falls into the ground and grows into a plant, and that plant drops more seeds that grow again and again. Valluvar says wanting things is like that seed: as long as we keep wanting, we keep getting planted into new lives, over and over.
university_explanation: The chapter that closes the ascetic section (Thuravaraviyal) opens by naming avaa (craving) as the vittu, the seed, of an unbroken chain of births (thavaap pirappu). The agricultural metaphor is exact: a seed holds the whole future plant, and craving holds the whole future of embodied existence, so destroying the seed leaves the cycle nothing to grow from. The word “enba” (“they say”) shows Valluvar reporting a consensus of the wise rather than inventing a doctrine, and the idea is indeed shared across Indian soteriologies: the Upanishadic teaching that desire determines rebirth, the Buddhist second noble truth that craving leads to renewed existence, and the Jain account of passions binding karma. Placed right after “Knowledge of Truth” (Meyyunarthal) and just before “Destiny” (Oozh), the chapter that ends Book 1, this chapter makes the uprooting of desire the practical summit of the renunciant’s path.

tamil:
வேண்டுங்கால் வேண்டும் பிறவாமை மற்றது
வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்.
transliteration:
Vendungaal vendum piravaamai matradhu
Vendaamai venda varum.
current_meaning: If you must desire something, desire freedom from rebirth. That freedom comes only when you desire to be free of desire.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you get just one wish. The smartest wish would be: “I wish I didn’t need any more wishes.” Valluvar says that is the one wish worth making, because it is the wish that sets you free.
university_explanation: The couplet repeats the verb vendu (“to want”) four times: vendungaal vendum … vendaamai venda. The verbal knot mirrors the paradox it describes. Valluvar admits that a person cannot simply switch off wanting, so he turns the power of desire against itself and makes piravaamai (non-birth, liberation) its one proper object. Parimelazhagar reads vendaamai as the settled state of desirelessness, so the means (wanting not to want) and the goal (not being born again) are joined. The same ‘desire for desirelessness’ paradox appears in the Buddhist distinction between wholesome aspiration (chanda) and craving (tanha), and in the Gita’s call to act without craving the fruits of action.

tamil:
வேண்டாமை அன்ன விழுச்செல்வம் ஈண்டில்லை
ஆண்டும் அஃதொப்பது இல்.
transliteration:
Vendaamai anna vizhuchchelvam eendillai
Aandum aqdhoppadhu il.
current_meaning: There is no treasure in this world as precious as freedom from desire. Even in the world beyond, nothing equals it.
elementary_explanation: A kid with a giant pile of toys who always wants more still feels poor. A kid who is happy with what they have feels rich. Valluvar says not wanting is the biggest treasure there is, bigger than anything here or even in heaven.
university_explanation: Vizhuchchelvam (“choicest wealth”) turns the idea of wealth inside out: a chapter on renunciation borrows the language of ownership to describe the absence of wanting. The pair eendu (“here”) and aandu (“there”) covers both this world and the heavenly worlds that ritual religion promised as rewards. Valluvar therefore ranks desirelessness above celestial pleasures, in line with the Upanishadic and Buddhist view that heaven is only a finer object of desire. The paradox that wanting less makes one richer shows up almost word for word in Seneca, in the Hadith on ‘richness of the soul’ and in Ben Zoma’s “Who is rich?”, which makes this one of the most cross-culturally shared couplets in the chapter.

tamil:
தூஉய்மை என்பது அவாவின்மை மற்றது
வாஅய்மை வேண்ட வரும்.
transliteration:
Thoouymai enbadhu avaavinmai matradhu
Vaaaimai venda varum.
current_meaning: Purity is nothing other than freedom from desire, and that freedom comes from longing for truth.
elementary_explanation: A glass of water looks clear when nothing is stirring it up. Your heart is “clean” when wanting isn’t stirring it. The way to keep it calm is to love what is true more than what is shiny.
university_explanation: Valluvar defines thooymai (purity) psychologically rather than ritually, not by baths, diet or caste observances but as avaavinmai, the absence of craving. The second line adds a cause: freedom from craving arises from desiring vaaymai. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan gloss vaaymai as meipporul, ultimate Reality, while Karunanidhi reads it as truthfulness. Either way the chapter keeps its strategy of redirecting desire, letting one longing, for truth, push out all lesser ones. The lengthened forms thoouymai and vaaaymai (alapedai, a metrical lengthening) bind the two key terms by sound as well as sense.

tamil:
அற்றவர் என்பார் அவாஅற்றார் மற்றையார்
அற்றாக அற்றது இலர்.
transliteration:
Atravar enbaar avaaatraar matraiyaar
Atraaga atradhu ilar.
current_meaning: Only those who have cut off desire deserve the name of true renunciants. Others, whatever they have given up, are not free in the same complete way.
elementary_explanation: Throwing your candy away doesn’t really count if you keep thinking about candy all day. Valluvar says the real “giver-upper” is the person who stopped wanting, not just the person who stopped having.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on atravar (“those who are cut off”, the renunciants) and avaa atraar (“those cut off from desire”), and ends by saying that others are not free in that full sense (atraaga atradhu ilar). Valluvar draws a sharp line between outward renunciation (robes, poverty, leaving home, the themes of the earlier chapter Thuravu) and inward renunciation. This extends his critique of the false ascetic in Chapter 28 (Koodaavozhukkam, “Imposture”). For Valluvar, freedom is measured by what one no longer wants, not by what one no longer owns.

tamil:
அஞ்சுவ தோரும் அறனே ஒருவனை
வஞ்சிப்ப தோரும் அவா.
transliteration:
Anjuva dhoorum arane oruvanai
Vanjippa dhoorum avaa.
current_meaning: To stand in fear of desire is itself virtue, because it is desire that deceives and ruins a person.
elementary_explanation: Some joke toys look like candy but have a spring inside that jumps out at you, so you learn to be careful of them. Valluvar says wanting things is a trick like that. It fools us, so being careful of it is part of being good.
university_explanation: The couplet frames the ethical life as vigilance: aran (virtue) here simply is the fearing (anjuvadhu) of avaa, because avaa is what vanjippadhu, what cheats and betrays a person. Commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan add that desire waits for a moment of weakness (sorvu) to strike, much as a thief waits for the watchman to nod off. The repeated expletive oorum gives the line a proverbial, almost incantatory rhythm. This picture of desire as a cunning inner enemy parallels the Gita’s portrait of kama as an “all-devouring” foe and the biblical image of sin crouching at the door.

tamil:
அவாவினை ஆற்ற அறுப்பின் தவாவினை
தான்வேண்டு மாற்றான் வரும்.
transliteration:
Avaavinai aatra aruppin thavaavinai
Thaan vendum aatraan varum.
current_meaning: If a person cuts off desire completely, the deeds that lead to an undying life will come to him just as he wishes.
elementary_explanation: When you stop grabbing at every toy in the store, your hands are finally free to hold what really matters. Valluvar says that when you drop all your wants, good deeds that last forever come to you easily.
university_explanation: Aatra aruppin, “if one cuts utterly”, insists on total rather than partial removal and echoes the chapter title’s aruththal (“cutting”). Thavaa vinai, “unfailing” or “imperishable action”, is glossed by commentators as the deeds that bring deathlessness, that is, liberation. The promise that these deeds arrive thaan vendum aatraan (“in the way he wishes”) holds a quiet irony: the person who has stopped wanting finally gets what he wants. The same paradox, that giving up self-will lines the will up with the good, appears in Stoic acceptance of fate, in the rabbinic “do His will as though it were your will”, and in the Katha Upanishad’s promise that the desireless mortal becomes immortal.

tamil:
அவாஇல்லார்க் கில்லாகுந் துன்பம் அஃதுண்டேல்
தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும்.
transliteration:
Avaa illaarkku illaagum thunbam aqdhundel
Thavaaadhu menmel varum.
current_meaning: Those without desire have no sorrow. Where desire exists, sorrow comes without fail, one after another.
elementary_explanation: Every time you want something you can’t have, you feel a little sad. If you want a hundred things, you get a hundred little sads. Want nothing, and the sads have nowhere to come from.
university_explanation: The couplet is a strict pair of conditions. For those without desire (avaa illaarkku), suffering ceases to exist (illaagum); if desire exists (aqdhundel), suffering comes thavaaadhu menmel, without fail, one upon another. The doubled menmel (“more and more, upon and upon”) imitates the way craving compounds, since each satisfied desire breeds new ones. This is the Kural’s closest approach to a formal statement of the Buddhist second noble truth, but Valluvar stays practical rather than metaphysical: he describes the lived economy of wanting, not a theory of dependent origination.

tamil:
இன்பம் இடையறா தீண்டும் அவாவென்னும்
துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்.
transliteration:
Inbam idaiyaraa theendum avaavennum
Thunbaththul thunbam kedin.
current_meaning: When desire, the worst of all sorrows, is destroyed, joy flows without a break, even in this life.
elementary_explanation: Imagine an itch you’ve had for so long that you forgot it was there. When it finally stops, you feel wonderful all the time. Valluvar says wanting is that itch, and when it’s gone, happiness just keeps going.
university_explanation: Valluvar calls avaa “thunbaththul thunbam”, the sorrow among sorrows, the one that gives rise to all the others. Removing it therefore does more than take away one pain: it dries up the source of every pain. The promised result, inbam idaiyaraadhu eendum, is unbroken joy “even here” (eendum), a this-worldly liberation comparable to the Upanishadic jivanmukta and to the Buddhist realization of nibbana in this very life. The joy is defined negatively, as what remains when craving stops. That lines up closely with the Buddhist third noble truth and with Epicurus’s definition of pleasure as freedom from disturbance.

tamil:
ஆரா இயற்கை அவாநீப்பின் அந்நிலையே
பேரா இயற்கை தரும்.
transliteration:
Aaraa iyarkai avaa neeppin annilaiye
Peraa iyarkai tharum.
current_meaning: Desire by nature can never be satisfied. Whoever casts it off gains, in that very moment, a nature that never changes: lasting bliss.
elementary_explanation: Trying to fill a bucket that has a hole in the bottom never works. You pour and pour, and it’s never full. Valluvar says wanting is that leaky bucket. Stop pouring into it, and you find a calm that never runs out.
university_explanation: The final couplet crowns the chapter with a mirrored wordplay: aaraa iyarkai (a nature that is never filled) against peraa iyarkai (a nature that never departs). Insatiability is what defines desire, and permanence is the reward for giving it up, the unchanging state that commentators identify with liberation (veedu). The word annilaiye (“in that very state” or “at that very moment”) suggests the reward is not postponed to some later heaven but is the same thing as the act of letting go. As the last couplet on renunciation before the chapter on Destiny that closes the Book of Virtue, it sums up Valluvar’s whole ascetic path: the endlessly hungry becomes the endlessly at peace.

tamil:
ஆகூழால் தோன்றும் அசைவின்மை கைப்பொருள்
போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி.
transliteration:
Aakoozhaal thondrum asaivinmai kaipporul
Pokoozhaal thondrum madi.
current_meaning: When fate is set on bringing wealth, it gives rise to tireless effort; when fate is set on taking wealth away, it gives rise to laziness.
elementary_explanation: Imagine two kids with the same homework. One suddenly feels full of energy and finishes it; the other feels sleepy and gives up. This kural says that even the energy or the sleepiness you feel can be part of your fate: good fortune shows up as hard work, and bad fortune shows up as laziness.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter with a subtle psychological claim: fate (ஊழ், uzh) does not merely deliver outcomes from outside but works through the agent’s own dispositions. ஆகூழ் (aakuzh, ‘fate of gaining’) manifests as அசைவின்மை (unflagging perseverance), while போகூழ் (pokuzh, ‘fate of losing’) manifests as மடி (sloth). This neatly reconciles the chapter with the Kural’s many praises of effort elsewhere (e.g. the later chapters on ஆள்வினையுடைமை): effort is praised, yet the very capacity to make effort is itself read as a sign of a favourable destiny. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar treat ஊழ் as the ripened fruit of past deeds (பழவினை), which makes the idea closer to karmic causation than to arbitrary luck. The structure anticipates the Stoic ‘co-fated’ reply to the Lazy Argument: outcome and effort are fated together, so fatalism is no excuse for idleness.

tamil:
பேதைப் படுக்கும் இழவூழ் அறிவகற்றும்
ஆகலூழ் உற்றக் கடை.
transliteration:
Pedhaip padukkum izhavoozh arivagatrum
Aagaloozh utrak kadai.
current_meaning: A fate of loss makes even a clever person act foolishly, while a fate of gain, when it arrives, widens a person’s understanding.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever had a day when you kept making silly mistakes, and another day when every answer just clicked? This kural says bad fortune can make even smart people act silly, and good fortune can make people seem wiser than usual.
university_explanation: The couplet extends the previous one from will to intellect: இழவூழ் (izhavuzh, ‘the fate of loss’) makes one பேதை (a fool), while ஆகலூழ் (aagaluzh, ‘the fate of increase’) அறிவு அகற்றும், widening or enlarging understanding. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan read அகற்றும் as ‘to expand’, not ‘to remove’. The idea is that judgement itself is vulnerable to fortune: brilliant people make ruinous decisions when their luck is turning. The same intuition appears across cultures as the sense that those heading for ruin are first robbed of good judgement, and in the biblical account of Ahithophel’s wise counsel being ‘defeated’ by divine design. Philosophically, it raises the question of moral luck: how far our rationality depends on circumstances we do not control.

tamil:
நுண்ணிய நூல்பல கற்பினும் மற்றுந்தன்
உண்மை யறிவே மிகும்.
transliteration:
Nunniya noolpala karpinum matrundhan
Unmai yarive migum.
current_meaning: However many subtle books a person studies, in the end it is the understanding that is truly their own, the portion allotted by fate, that prevails.
elementary_explanation: You can give a pencil to every child in class, but each one will still draw in their own way. This kural says that reading many clever books helps, but in the end a person’s own natural understanding decides how they really think and act.
university_explanation: The key phrase is உண்மை அறிவு (unmai arivu): literally ‘the knowledge that truly is’ one’s own, which commentators gloss as the understanding given by ஊழ், as opposed to what is acquired from books (நூல்). Valluvar is not dismissing learning; he devotes whole chapters to கல்வி (learning). He is noting that learning is filtered through an innate capacity it cannot fully override. The Gita makes a parallel claim that even the learned act according to their own nature (prakṛti), and Heraclitus’ fragment that character is a person’s daimon points the same way. Modern debates on nature versus nurture, and on the limits of education, are a secular version of the same observation.

tamil:
இருவேறு உலகத்து இயற்கை திருவேறு
தெள்ளிய ராதலும் வேறு.
transliteration:
Iruveru ulagaththu iyarkai thiruveru
Thelliya raadhalum veru.
current_meaning: Fate works in the world in two different ways: becoming wealthy is one thing, and becoming wise is quite another.
elementary_explanation: Some kids are great at sports and others are great at math, and being good at one doesn’t make you good at the other. This kural says money and wisdom work the same way: being rich and being wise come from different kinds of luck, so one doesn’t guarantee the other.
university_explanation: The couplet makes an observation anyone can check: wealth (திரு, thiru, also the name of the goddess of fortune) and clear wisdom (தெள்ளியர் ஆதல்) are handed out on separate tracks. The rich are often not wise, and the wise are often not rich. Commentators read இருவேறு இயற்கை as two distinct operations of ஊழ். Indian folk tradition expresses the same idea as the old rivalry between Lakshmi (wealth) and Saraswati (learning). Ecclesiastes’ remark that bread is not always to the wise nor riches to the understanding, the Talmudic teaching on sustenance depending on mazal rather than merit, and Aristotle’s puzzle about fortunate fools all record the same gap between intelligence and worldly reward.

tamil:
நல்லவை எல்லாஅந் தீயவாம் தீயவும்
நல்லவாம் செல்வம் செயற்கு.
transliteration:
Nallavai ellaaan theeyavaam theeyavum
Nallavaam selvam seyarku.
current_meaning: In the pursuit of wealth, fate can turn every favourable circumstance into an unfavourable one, and every unfavourable circumstance into a favourable one.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes you plan a picnic on a sunny day and it rains anyway. Other times you get stuck indoors and end up finding something wonderful. This kural says that when it comes to making money, luck can flip good chances into bad ones and bad chances into good ones.
university_explanation: Commentators take நல்லவை and தீயவை here as circumstances favourable or unfavourable to earning, such as the right time, place, means and partners, rather than moral good and evil. Solomon Pappaiah glosses the kural this way: even with the right time, place and trade, an adverse fate brings loss, and even without them a favourable fate brings profit. The couplet warns against over-confidence in planning, since the same conditions can produce opposite results depending on forces beyond calculation. Across traditions this becomes the theme of reversal: the Qur'an’s ‘perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you’, Rabbi Akiva’s night journey, and Boethius’ turning wheel of Fortune.

tamil:
பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல உய்த்துச்
சொரியினும் போகா தம.
transliteration:
Pariyinum aagaavaam paalalla uyththuch
Choriyinum pogaa thama.
current_meaning: What fate has not made yours will not stay with you, however anxiously you guard it; and what fate has made yours will not leave you, even if you carry it off and throw it away.
elementary_explanation: Imagine holding sand tightly in your fist: it still slips out. Now imagine a boomerang: you throw it away and it comes back. This kural says things that aren’t meant for you slip away however hard you hold on, and things that are meant for you come back even if you throw them away.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on பால் (paal), ‘share’ or ‘portion’, the same word used for the three books of the Kural. Things outside one’s allotted share (பாலல்ல) cannot be kept even with painful guarding (பரியினும்), and things within it (தம) will not leave even if deliberately poured out (உய்த்துச் சொரியினும்). It is an extreme statement of possession as destiny. Greek tradition gives a near-perfect illustration in Polycrates’ ring, which was thrown into the sea and came back inside a fish. The ethical point, drawn out by Stoics like Epictetus, is that anxious clinging is irrational: one should hold possessions loosely, as things on loan.

tamil:
வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகையல்லால் கோடி
தொகுத்தார்க்கு துய்த்தல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Vaguththaan vaguththa vagaiyallaal kodi
Thoguththaarkku thuyththal aridhu.
current_meaning: Even those who amass crores of wealth can enjoy it only to the extent that the Ordainer has ordained; beyond that, enjoyment is impossible.
elementary_explanation: You could fill a whole room with candy, but if you have a toothache you can’t eat any of it. This kural says that piling up huge amounts of money doesn’t mean you’ll get to enjoy it; how much you actually enjoy is decided by fate.
university_explanation: The striking phrase வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை (‘the way apportioned by the Apportioner’) is one of the few places where Valluvar speaks of fate through an agent. Commentators differ on whether வகுத்தான் means God or the impersonal law of past deeds. The kural separates possession from enjoyment (துய்த்தல்): accumulation is within human reach, but the capacity to enjoy is allotted. The same gap appears in Ecclesiastes’ rich man to whom God does not give ‘power to eat thereof’, in Jesus’ parable of the rich fool, and in the myth of Midas starving amid gold. This makes the couplet a critique of hoarding as well as a statement about fate.

tamil:
துறப்பார்மன் துப்புர வில்லார் உறற்பால
ஊட்டா கழியு மெனின்.
transliteration:
Thurappaarman thuppura villaar urarpaala
Oottaa kazhiyu menin.
current_meaning: The destitute, who have nothing to enjoy, would renounce the world, if only fate let the sufferings destined for them pass without making them undergo them.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone with an empty lunchbox. You might think it would be easy for them to say ‘I don’t need lunch.’ But they still feel hungry. This kural says poor people would give up wanting things and become monks, but fate still makes them feel the troubles they are meant to go through, so they can’t let go.
university_explanation: This is the chapter’s most compressed and most debated couplet. துப்புரவு (thuppuravu) means the means of enjoyment; those without it (the destitute) would seem to be natural renunciants, since they have nothing to give up. The particle மன் signals an unrealised possibility: they *would* renounce, *if* the sufferings that are theirs to experience (உறற்பால) passed away without being fed to them (ஊட்டா கழியும்). The implication is ironic: poverty does not automatically produce detachment, because fate still insists that its allotted pains be tasted. This fits the karmic principle, shared with Buddhism and Jainism, that ripened deeds must be experienced and cannot simply be skipped.

tamil:
நன்றாங்கால் நல்லவாக் காண்பவர் அன்றாங்கால்
அல்லற் படுவ தெவன்.
transliteration:
Nandraangaal nallavaak kaanbavar andraangaal
Allar paduva thevan.
current_meaning: Those who take good fortune happily as good when it comes, why should they be distressed when misfortune comes, since both arise from the same fate?
elementary_explanation: When you win a game you say ‘Yay, lucky me!’ So when you lose, why get so upset? Both winning and losing come from the same luck. This kural asks us to take the bad days as calmly as we enjoy the good ones.
university_explanation: The couplet is a rhetorical question with a Stoic edge. If good fortune (நன்று) and misfortune (அன்று) both come from ஊழ், then welcoming one and lamenting the other is inconsistent. Mu. Varadarasan glosses it as good deeds and evil deeds ripening, which ties the couplet to karmic reasoning. The ethical advice is equanimity (சமநிலை): accept both outcomes as coming from one source. It is closely echoed in Job’s reply to his wife, in the Mishnah’s rule to bless God for the bad as for the good, in the Gita’s teaching on bearing pleasure and pain alike, in the Buddha’s eight worldly conditions, and in Nietzsche’s amor fati.

tamil:
ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள மற்றொன்று
சூழினுந் தான்முந் துறும்.
transliteration:
Oozhir peruvali yaavula matrondru
Soozhinun thaanmun thurum.
current_meaning: What is mightier than fate? Even when a person devises another way to escape it, fate gets there first.
elementary_explanation: Imagine playing tag with someone who always knows which way you’ll run and is already waiting there. That’s how this kural describes fate: whatever clever path you choose to avoid it, fate is already there ahead of you.
university_explanation: The chapter, and with it the whole Book of Virtue (அறத்துப்பால்), ends on a rhetorical question: ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள, ‘what is of greater strength than fate?’ The second line gives the reason: even if one plans (சூழினும்) another course, fate itself arrives first (தான் முந்துறும்). The positioning matters. After thirty-seven chapters on virtue, Valluvar closes by acknowledging the limits of human agency. Book 2 (Porul) then opens with vigorous chapters on effort, and later ones such as ஆள்வினையுடைமை (e.g. Kural 620) even assert that tireless striving can push fate aside. The tension is intended, and it mirrors the Stoic formula that fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling, as well as the Oedipus myth, in which the flight from prophecy is what fulfils it.

tamil:
படைகுடி கூழ்அமைச்சு நட்பரண் ஆறும்
உடையான் அரசருள் ஏறு.
transliteration:
Padai kudi koozh amaichu natparan aarum
Udaiyaan arasarul eru.
current_meaning: A ruler who possesses all six parts of a state — an army, a loyal people, resources, wise ministers, allies, and strong fortifications — stands among kings like a lion among beasts.
elementary_explanation: Think of a strong table that needs all its legs to stand. A kingdom needs six “legs”: soldiers, happy people, food and money, good helpers, friends, and strong walls. A king who has all six is like the lion — the strongest of all the kings.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the Book of Polity not with the king’s personality but with a structural inventory of the state: padai (army), kudi (citizenry), koozh (food/revenue), amaichu (ministry), natpu (alliances), and aran (fortification). This six-limbed model closely parallels the saptanga (“seven-limbed”) theory of the state found in Kautilya’s Arthashastra, minus the king himself — who in the Kural is the one who ‘possesses’ the six, making him the integrating seventh element. The image of the ‘eru’ (a male lion or bull, the pre-eminent male of its kind) frames kingship as excellence in a competitive field of rulers rather than divine right. The chapter structure of the Porutpaal then follows this list, with later chapters devoted to each limb (army, fortress, friendship, ministers), so this kural functions as a table of contents for the whole book of statecraft.

tamil:
அஞ்சாமை ஈகை அறிவூக்கம் இந்நான்கும்
எஞ்சாமை வேந்தர்க் கியல்பு.
transliteration:
Anjaamai eegai arivookkam innaankum
Enjaamai vendhark kiyalbu.
current_meaning: Fearlessness, generosity, wisdom, and energetic drive — never to be lacking in these four is the true nature of a king.
elementary_explanation: A good team captain is brave, shares with everyone, knows what to do, and never gets lazy. This kural says a real king must have all four of these — and never run out of any of them.
university_explanation: Having described the external assets of the state, Valluvar now names the four inner qualities of the ruler: anjaamai (fearlessness), eegai (liberality), arivu (wisdom), and ookkam (energy or zeal). The key word is enjaamai — ‘without deficiency’ — which makes the standard one of constancy: a king who is brave in one crisis but timid in the next, or generous only when convenient, does not meet it. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar pair the qualities functionally: courage and energy to act, wisdom to decide rightly, and generosity to bind people to the ruler. The list resembles the Bhagavad Gita’s catalogue of kshatriya traits and Plato’s requirements for the philosopher-ruler, suggesting a widely shared intuition that rulership needs both a warrior’s nerve and a sage’s judgment.

tamil:
தூங்காமை கல்வி துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றும்
நீங்கா நிலனான் பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Thoongaamai kalvi thunivudaimai immoondrum
Neengaa nilanaan bavarkku.
current_meaning: Alertness that never delays, learning, and firm resolve — these three must never leave those who rule a land.
elementary_explanation: A good lifeguard never falls asleep on duty, knows how to swim and rescue, and jumps in bravely when needed. A ruler needs the same three things: stay awake, keep learning, and be brave enough to act.
university_explanation: Thoongaamai literally means ‘not sleeping’, and the commentators read it as freedom from sloth and delay — prompt action when action is due. Kalvi (learning) and thunivu (decisive courage) complete the triad, and the verb neengaa (‘must not depart’) again stresses that these are permanent dispositions, not occasional performances. The combination is significant: learning without resolve produces a hesitant ruler, and resolve without learning produces a reckless one, while both fail without vigilance. Kautilya’s Arthashastra makes the same point in its timetable for the king, which divides the day and night into tasks and insists that the king ‘shall ever be wakeful’.

tamil:
அறனிழுக்கா தல்லவை நீக்கி மறனிழுக்கா
மானம் உடைய தரசு.
transliteration:
Aranizhukkaa thallavai neekki maranizhukkaa
Maanam udaiya tharasu.
current_meaning: True kingship never swerves from righteousness, removes whatever is unrighteous from the land, and holds to an honour that never falls short in courage.
elementary_explanation: A good referee always follows the rules, sends off players who cheat, and is brave enough to make hard calls. This kural says a real ruler is like that: always fair, stops wrongdoing, and never loses courage or self-respect.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a pair of parallel negatives: aran izhukkaa (not slipping from dharma) and maran izhukkaa (not slipping from martial valour), bound together by maanam — honour or self-respect. Between them sits the positive duty allavai neekki, ‘removing what is not right’, which commentators read both as the king avoiding vice himself and as his suppressing wrongdoing in the realm. The effect is to insist that courage and justice must travel together: valour without righteousness becomes tyranny, while righteousness without valour cannot protect anyone. This coupling of justice and courage has a close analogue in Cicero’s claim that greatness of spirit divorced from justice is a vice rather than a virtue.

tamil:
இயற்றலும் ஈட்டலுங் காத்தலும் காத்த
வகுத்தலும் வல்ல தரசு.
transliteration:
Iyatralum eettalung kaaththalum kaaththa
Vaguththalum valla tharasu.
current_meaning: A true government is one skilled in creating sources of wealth, gathering it in, safeguarding it, and then distributing what has been safeguarded wisely.
elementary_explanation: Think of a farmer who plants seeds, harvests the crop, stores it safely in a barn, and then shares it out so everyone has food all year. A good ruler does the same with the country’s wealth: make it, collect it, protect it, and share it fairly.
university_explanation: This is the Kural’s compact theory of public finance, expressed as four verbs: iyatral (generating new sources of revenue), eettal (collecting), kaaththal (guarding), and vaguththal (apportioning or allocating). The sequence is cyclical — well-allocated spending produces the prosperity from which new revenue is generated — and it treats wealth as a means of governance rather than a royal possession. Commentators note that vaguththal implies planned allocation among competing ends (defence, welfare, religious and civic works), not merely generosity. The same logic appears in Kalidasa’s praise of King Dilipa, who taxed his people only as the sun draws up water, in order to return it a thousandfold as rain.

tamil:
காட்சிக் கெளியன் கடுஞ்சொல்லன் அல்லனேல்
மீக்கூறும் மன்னன் நிலம்.
transliteration:
Kaatchik keliyan kadunjollan allanel
Meekkoorum mannan nilam.
current_meaning: If a king is easy for his people to approach and is not harsh in speech, the whole world will praise his land.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a school principal whose door is always open and who speaks kindly to every student. Everyone would say that’s a great school! A king who is easy to meet and never speaks rudely makes his whole country admired.
university_explanation: Kaatchikku eliyan — ‘easy to be seen’ — names the political virtue of accessibility: a ruler who can be reached by ordinary petitioners without layers of gatekeepers. The second condition, not being kadunjollan (a speaker of harsh words), concerns the manner of the encounter once access is granted. The reward is striking: it is the land (nilam), not merely the king, that the world exalts, implying that a ruler’s approachability shapes the reputation of the whole polity. Kautilya warns in almost identical terms that a king who makes himself inaccessible breeds confusion and public disaffection, and Islamic tradition records a hadith threatening divine seclusion from the ruler who secludes himself from his people.

tamil:
இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க வல்லார்க்குத் தன்சொலால்
தான்கண் டனைத்திவ் வுலகு.
transliteration:
Insolaal eeththalikka vallaarkkuth thansolaal
Thaankan danaiththiv vulagu.
current_meaning: For the ruler who can give with kind words and protect those who come to him, the world becomes just as he wishes it to be, praising him and following his word.
elementary_explanation: When a friend shares their snacks and says something nice while doing it, everyone wants to be on their team. A king who gives generously, speaks kindly, and protects people finds that the whole world is happy to follow him.
university_explanation: The kural joins three verbs — speaking sweetly (insol), giving (eeththal), and protecting (alittal) — and makes their combination the source of consent. The second line is compressed: ‘the world becomes as he sees it by his word’, which commentators such as Parimelazhagar read as the world both praising him and conforming to his intentions. The insight is that legitimacy is earned through the manner as well as the substance of benefaction: gifts given with contempt create resentment, whereas gifts with kind words create loyalty. This closely matches the Buddhist ‘bases of fellowship’ (generosity, kind speech, beneficial help, consistency) and the counsel Rehoboam’s elders gave him — ‘speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever’.

tamil:
முறைசெய்து காப்பாற்றும் மன்னவன் மக்கட்கு
இறையென்று வைக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
Muraiseydhu kaappaatrum mannavan makkatku
Iraiyendru vaikkap padum.
current_meaning: The king who rules with justice and protects his people will be regarded by them as a god.
elementary_explanation: When a lifeguard keeps everyone safe and is always fair, the swimmers look up to them like a hero. This kural says a ruler who is fair and protects everyone is looked up to by the people almost like God.
university_explanation: The word irai carries a deliberate double meaning — both ‘lord/king’ and ‘God’ — and the chapter title Iraimaatchi itself plays on it. Crucially, Valluvar makes divinity conditional: the king is ‘placed’ (vaikkappadum) as god by the people only because he does murai (justice, due order) and protects them. This inverts the claim of inherent divine kingship found in texts like the Laws of Manu, grounding sacral status in performance rather than birth. Aristotle’s remark that a person of pre-eminent virtue ‘may truly be deemed a God among men’ and Psalm 82’s address to judges as ‘gods’ who must defend the poor show the same conditional logic.

tamil:
செவிகைப்பச் சொற்பொறுக்கும் பண்புடை வேந்தன்
கவிகைக்கீழ்த் தங்கும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Sevikaippach sorporukkum panbudai vendhan
Kavigaikkeezhth thangum ulagu.
current_meaning: The whole world will shelter beneath the royal umbrella of a king gracious enough to bear words that are bitter to his ears.
elementary_explanation: Good medicine often tastes bad, but it makes you better. A wise king listens even when someone tells him an unpleasant truth. Because of that, everyone feels safe living under his rule.
university_explanation: Sevi kaippa — ‘so that the ear tastes bitterness’ — is a vivid synaesthetic image for criticism that is unpleasant to hear. The commentators specify that these are the admonitions of wise elders and ministers, whose duty (developed in the later chapter on ‘Seeking the Help of the Great’) is to rebuke the king when needed. The kavigai (royal parasol) is the symbol of sovereign protection, so the kural’s claim is that tolerance of criticism is not a weakness but the condition under which the whole world will rest securely under the ruler’s shade. Vidura’s warning in the Mahabharata that speakers and hearers of unpleasant but healing words are rare, and Marcus Aurelius’ readiness to be corrected, express the same insight.

tamil:
கொடையளி செங்கோல் குடியோம்பல் நான்கும்
உடையானாம் வேந்தர்க் கொளி.
transliteration:
Kodaiyali sengol kudiyombal naangum
Udaiyaanaam vendhark koli.
current_meaning: The one who has these four — generosity, compassion, a just sceptre, and care for his people — is the light among kings.
elementary_explanation: In a dark room, a lamp helps everyone see. This kural says the best king is like a lamp for all other kings, because he gives generously, is kind, rules fairly, and takes care of his people.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with a second set of four, this time outward-facing: kodai (gifts), ali (grace or compassion), sengol (the ‘straight sceptre’, i.e., just rule), and kudi ombal (nurturing the people). Where 382 described the king’s inner capacities, this kural describes their effects on subjects, and it crowns the one who has them as oli — the lamp or radiance — of kings, a model by which other rulers are measured. The sengol (straight sceptre) is a central symbol of Tamil political thought, contrasted with the kodungol (crooked sceptre) of the tyrant in later chapters. The image of the just ruler as light recurs in David’s last words in 2 Samuel, and the Hebrew Bible’s ‘sceptre of righteousness’ offers a remarkably close verbal parallel.

tamil:
கற்க கசடறக் கற்பவை கற்றபின்
நிற்க அதற்குத் தக.
transliteration:
Karka kasadarak karpavai katrapin
Nirka adharkuth thaga.
current_meaning: Learn what is worth learning, and learn it thoroughly, without flaw or gap. Then, once you have learned it, live in a way that matches what you have learned.
elementary_explanation: Imagine learning all the rules of football perfectly but then cheating in the game. That would make the learning pointless. This kural says two things: learn good things properly, then actually live by them.
university_explanation: The chapter on Kalvi opens with a two-step command. The first is கற்க கசடற: learn so that no flaw (kasadu) is left, which traditional commentators such as Parimelazhagar read as choosing the right texts and also removing one's own mental faults through study. The second is நிற்க அதற்குத் தக: stand, or remain, in conduct fitting to that learning. The verb நிற்க (to stand) is significant, because it pictures learning as a place one lives in and not only a set of facts one holds. Because the chapter sits in the Porul section, just after the chapter on kingship, this is also advice to rulers: a king's learning is shown in how he governs, not in how much he can recite. The same link between knowing and doing appears across many traditions, from the Epistle of James to the Stoic Epictetus.

tamil:
எண்ணென்ப ஏனை எழுத்தென்ப இவ்விரண்டும்
கண்ணென்ப வாழும் உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Ennenba enai ezhuthenba ivvirandum
Kannenba vaazhum uyirkku.
current_meaning: What are called numbers, and the other thing called letters: the wise say these two are the eyes of every living person.
elementary_explanation: You have two eyes to see the world. Valluvar says your mind also has two eyes: numbers and letters. Maths and reading let you understand things you could never see without them.
university_explanation: This kural reduces the whole of learning to two basic disciplines, எண் (en, number and calculation) and எழுத்து (ezhuthu, letters and literacy), and calls them the two eyes of human life. Commentators widened the terms. Parimelazhagar took en to cover arithmetic and the sciences such as astronomy, and ezhuthu to cover grammar and literature. The modern commentator Solomon Pappaiah even glosses them as science and the arts. The repeated என்ப ('they say') presents this as settled wisdom, not personal opinion. The image of eyes prepares for the next kural, where lacking learning is compared to having sores instead of eyes. Remarkably, Aeschylus' Prometheus names the very same pair, numbers and the combining of letters, as the founding gifts of civilization.

tamil:
கண்ணுடையர் என்பவர் கற்றோர் முகத்திரண்டு
புண்ணுடையர் கல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Kannudaiyar enbavar katror mugaththirandu
Punnudaiyar kallaa thavar.
current_meaning: Only the learned can truly be said to have eyes. Those without learning merely carry two sores on their face.
elementary_explanation: Two holes in your face are not the same as seeing. If you never learn anything, your eyes look at the world but understand nothing. Valluvar says a person who learns has real eyes.
university_explanation: Continuing the eye metaphor of Kural 392, Valluvar reaches one of the harshest images in the chapter. The unlearned person's eyes are புண் (pun), wounds or sores: openings in the face that do nothing and may even be painful. The contrast rests on the difference between physical sight and understanding. Kalaignar's commentary draws the corollary that a learned person without physical sight still 'has eyes', while an unlearned person with sight does not. The rhetoric is deliberately provocative. It belongs to a statecraft section meant to push kings and citizens toward education, and the following chapter, Kallaamai (Ignorance), develops the same harshness. Similar contrasts between seeing eyes and a seeing mind run through the Gospels, the Qur'an and Plato.

tamil:
உவப்பத் தலைக்கூடி உள்ளப் பிரிதல்
அனைத்தே புலவர் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Uvappath thalaikkoodi ullap piridhal
Anaiththe pulavar thozhil.
current_meaning: The mark of the learned is this: people rejoice when they meet them, and when they part, people keep thinking of them and long to meet again.
elementary_explanation: Think of a teacher or grandparent whose stories you love. When they come, you are happy. When they leave, you wish they could stay longer. Valluvar says that is how learned people make everyone feel.
university_explanation: Here Valluvar moves from the value of learning to its social effect. The புலவர் (pulavar, the learned or poet-scholar) is defined by an experience they create in others: உவப்ப, gladness at meeting, and உள்ளப் பிரிதல், parting in a way that leaves people thinking of them. The word தொழில் (thozhil, occupation or characteristic work) suggests that bringing joy through conversation is the scholar's real 'profession'. Commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan gloss the second half as others wondering when they will see such a person again. The kural implicitly contrasts true learning, which is generous and delightful, with pedantry that makes people glad to leave. Greek tradition offers vivid parallels, from Odysseus spellbinding the Phaeacians to Alcibiades' account of being enchanted by Socrates' words.

tamil:
உடையார்முன் இல்லார்போல் ஏக்கற்றுங் கற்றார்
கடையரே கல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Udaiyaarmun illaarpol ekkatrum katraar
Kadaiyare kallaa thavar.
current_meaning: Those who humbly stand before their teachers, eager as the poor before the rich, and so gain learning, are truly superior. Those who will not stoop to learn are the lowest of all.
elementary_explanation: A hungry child waits eagerly for food. A good student waits just as eagerly to learn from a teacher, and is not too proud to ask. The kural says being too proud to learn is what really makes you low.
university_explanation: The kural draws on a social image any reader would recognize: the needy person standing anxiously (ஏக்கற்று) before the wealthy. It applies that image to the student before the teacher. What looks like humiliation is really the road to greatness, since those who learn this way are the truly elevated (கற்றார்), while those who refuse to learn are கடையர், the lowest. Solomon Pappaiah reads the second line as condemning those who are ashamed to stand and learn, which makes pride the real barrier to education. The inversion of rank is typical of Valluvar: outward humility produces inner eminence. Many traditions make the same point, from the Gita's call to approach a teacher with submission (echoed in the Sanskrit maxim vidyā dadāti vinayam, 'learning gives humility') to the Mishnah's warning that the shy or ashamed cannot learn.

tamil:
தொட்டனைத் தூறும் மணற்கேணி மாந்தர்க்குக்
கற்றனைத் தூறும் அறிவு.
transliteration:
Thottanaith thoorum manarkeni maandharkkuk
Katranaith thoorum arivu.
current_meaning: A well dug in sandy ground gives water in proportion to how deep it is dug. In the same way, understanding wells up in a person in proportion to how much they have learned.
elementary_explanation: When you dig a hole at the beach, water starts to seep in, and the deeper you dig, the more water comes. Your mind works the same way: the more you learn, the more wisdom flows out of you.
university_explanation: This is perhaps the most quoted kural of the chapter. It rests on a precise agricultural image from the Tamil landscape: the மணற்கேணி, a shallow well dug in sandy riverbed or soil, where groundwater seeps in more strongly the deeper one digs. The parallel verbs தொட்டனை ('as much as dug') and கற்றனை ('as much as learned') set up an exact proportion, and the shared verb ஊறும் ('springs, oozes up') links the two halves. The point is that wisdom (அறிவு, arivu) is not poured in from outside but springs up from within, released by the labour of study. It also implies that learning has no fixed end, since there is always more water below. Parallels range from Proverbs' 'wellspring of wisdom' and the Mishnah's 'ever-flowing spring' to Pope's 'Pierian spring'.

tamil:
யாதானும் நாடாமால் ஊராமால் என்னொருவன்
சாந்துணையுங் கல்லாத வாறு.
transliteration:
Yaadhaanum naadaamaal ooraamaal ennoruvan
Saanthunaiyum kallaadha vaaru.
current_meaning: To a learned person, every country becomes their own country and every town their own town. So why would anyone go without learning, right up to the day they die?
elementary_explanation: A good doctor or teacher can move to any town and still be welcomed and needed. What you learn goes with you everywhere and makes you at home anywhere. So why would anyone ever stop learning?
university_explanation: The kural is built as a rhetorical question. Its premise is that for the learned, யாதானும் நாடாம், ஊராம் (any land is their land, any town is their town), because learning makes a person welcome and useful anywhere. Its conclusion asks why anyone would remain unlearned சாந்துணையும், 'even until death'. That phrase quietly adds the idea of lifelong learning: there is no age at which study becomes pointless. In the Porul section's concern with the practical world, this is an argument from utility. Land and local status can be lost, but learning is portable citizenship. The first idea matches the Sanskrit maxim that a scholar is honoured everywhere, and the second matches Solon's line about growing old while always learning.

tamil:
ஒருமைக்கண் தான்கற்ற கல்வி ஒருவற்கு
எழுமையும் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Orumaikkan thaankatra kalvi oruvarku
Ezhumaiyum emaap pudaiththu.
current_meaning: The learning a person gains in one lifetime has the power to protect and help them through seven lifetimes to come.
elementary_explanation: Planting a tree helps you, your children and your grandchildren long after you have gone. Valluvar says learning is even bigger than that: what you learn now keeps helping you far into the future, even into future lives.
university_explanation: This kural draws on the Indian framework of rebirth. ஒருமை (orumai, 'one birth') is set against எழுமை (ezhumai, 'seven births'), a conventional expression for a long chain of future lives. The key word ஏமாப்பு (emaappu) means protection, security or support, so learning is pictured as a lasting safeguard that goes with the soul. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah follow the traditional rebirth reading. Kalaignar reinterprets it more secularly as learning that protects seven generations of a family. The kural fits the chapter's larger claim that learning, unlike other goods, is not used up or lost. Similar ideas appear in the Gita's teaching that a yogi's progress carries over into the next life and in Plato's theory that learning is recollection from earlier existence.

tamil:
தாமின் புறுவது உலகின் புறக்கண்டு
காமுறுவர் கற்றறிந் தார்.
transliteration:
Thaaminburuvadhu ulaginburak kandu
Kaamuruvar katrarindhaar.
current_meaning: When the learned see that the learning which delights them also delights the whole world, they come to love learning even more.
elementary_explanation: When you discover a great story and tell your friends, they love it too, and that makes you want to find even more stories. Learning works like that. Sharing it makes everyone happy, so you want to learn more.
university_explanation: The kural describes a self-reinforcing cycle of joy. The learned find pleasure (இன்புறுவது) in their own knowledge, then see that the same knowledge brings pleasure to the world (உலகு இன்புற). That discovery makes them desire (காமுறுவர்) learning all the more. Valluvar's use of kaamam, a word more often tied to love and desire, is striking: learning becomes a passion. The kural suggests that the highest motive for study is neither prestige nor profit but shared delight, which makes knowledge a social good. The idea is echoed in Seneca's statement that he learns only in order to teach, and in the Mishnah and hadith traditions that praise those who learn in order to share.

tamil:
கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி யொருவற்கு
மாடல்ல மற்றை யவை.
transliteration:
Kedil vizhuchchelvam kalvi oruvarku
Maadalla matraiyavai.
current_meaning: Learning is the one excellent wealth that can never be destroyed. Compared with it, all other possessions are not true wealth at all.
elementary_explanation: Toys can break, money can be lost, and a house can burn down. What you have learned stays in your head, and no one can steal it. That is why Valluvar calls learning the best treasure of all.
university_explanation: The chapter ends with its thesis. Learning is கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம், 'imperishable, excellent wealth', and all other things are மாடு அல்ல, 'not wealth'. மாடு (maadu) is an old Tamil word for wealth that originally meant cattle, the earliest form of property, which gives the claim an archaic force. The argument works on two levels. Materially, learning cannot be stolen, taxed, destroyed or divided. Evaluatively, only learning deserves the name 'wealth' at all. Placing this conclusion in the Porul (Wealth) section is pointed, since Valluvar redefines the very wealth that section is about. The same claim appears almost word for word in the Sanskrit verse on vidyā-dhana, the wealth of knowledge that thieves cannot steal and kings cannot seize.

tamil:
அரங்கின்றி வட்டாடி யற்றே நிரம்பிய
நூலின்றிக் கோட்டி கொளல்.
transliteration:
Arangindri vattaadi yatre nirampiya
Noolindrik kotti kolal.
current_meaning: To address an assembly of the learned without having fully mastered the texts of learning is like playing at dice without a board marked out.
elementary_explanation: Imagine trying to play a board game when nobody has drawn the board. You can roll the dice, but none of your moves mean anything. This kural says that speaking in front of wise people when you haven’t really studied is exactly like that: lots of movement, no real game.
university_explanation: The image is precise: vattu (dice or game pieces) moved without an arangu (the ruled board or square) produce motion without rules, and therefore without meaning or result. Kotti (an assembly, a learned gathering) is the arena of debate, and nirampiya nool (complete, fully mastered texts) is the board that gives structure to every move. Parimelazhagar reads the verse as a warning to one who enters discussion with no framework of learning: his words, however energetic, have nothing to be scored against. The chapter thus opens by defining ignorance not as silence but as ungrounded speech. Across traditions, the parallel concern is the would-be teacher or debater who speaks confidently while ‘understanding neither what they say’ (1 Timothy), the Qur’anic ban on pursuing what one has no knowledge of, and Plato’s critique of the rhetorician who persuades without knowing.

tamil:
கல்லாதான் சொற்கா முறுதல் முலையிரண்டும்
இல்லாதாள் பெண்காமுற் றற்று.
transliteration:
Kallaadhaan sorkaa murudhal mulaiyirandum
Illaadhaal penkaamut rattru.
current_meaning: For an unlearned man to long to be heard as a speaker is like a woman without breasts longing to be desired as a woman.
elementary_explanation: Some people want everyone to listen to them, but they haven’t learned anything worth saying. Valluvar uses a blunt comparison from his own time: it’s like wanting to be admired for something you simply don’t have. The wish is there, but the thing that would make it come true is missing.
university_explanation: Sorkaamurudhal is a craving for speech — specifically the desire to be admired for eloquence in an assembly. Valluvar’s simile, jarring to modern ears, is built on the conventions of classical Tamil poetics, where breasts are a standard marker of feminine attractiveness; the point is structural rather than a comment on women: a desire whose necessary basis is absent is futile and invites ridicule. Learning is to speech what that physical attribute is to erotic appeal in the poetic code. Parallel traditions frame the same pathology as the fool who ‘hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself’ (Proverbs 18:2), the Gita’s ‘men of small knowledge’ attached to flowery words, and the Dhammapada’s reminder that one is not wise because one speaks much. Modern readers may note the simile’s gendered framing as a product of its poetic era.

tamil:
கல்லா தவரும் நனிநல்லர் கற்றார்முன்
சொல்லா திருக்கப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Kallaa thavarum naninallar katraarmun
Sollaa thirukkap perin.
current_meaning: Even the unlearned are counted very good, if only they can keep from speaking in the presence of the learned.
elementary_explanation: If you don’t know much about a subject and you’re with experts, the smartest thing you can do is stay quiet and listen. People will actually think well of you for it. Talking would show what you don’t know; silence protects you and lets you learn.
university_explanation: The irony of nani nallar (‘exceedingly good’) is gentle but pointed: the unlearned person’s one available virtue is restraint. Parimelazhagar notes that silence both conceals the defect and avoids the harm of error. The verse inverts the previous kural — where the unlearned craved speech, here he is redeemed by abstaining from it. This is one of the most widely shared moral intuitions across cultures: Proverbs 17:28 (‘Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise’), Rabbi Akiva’s ‘a fence for wisdom is silence’, and the famous Sanskrit maxim of Bhartrhari that silence is the ornament of the unlearned in an assembly of scholars, which is an almost exact parallel. The Buddhist corpus adds the self-knowledge dimension: the fool who knows he is a fool is to that extent wise.

tamil:
கல்லாதான் ஒட்பம் கழியநன் றாயினும்
கொள்ளார் அறிவுடை யார்.
transliteration:
Kallaadhaan otpam kazhiyanan raayinum
Kollaar arivudai yaar.
current_meaning: Even if an unlearned man’s cleverness happens to be exceedingly good, the wise will not accept it as sound.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes a person who never studied says something that sounds really smart. Wise people still don’t rely on it, because it’s a lucky hit, not something the person truly understands. Next time the same person may be completely wrong, and they won’t know the difference.
university_explanation: Otpam denotes native sharpness or cleverness; kazhiya nandru (‘exceedingly good’) concedes that it may even be impressive. Yet the wise (arivudaiyaar) do not ‘take’ (kollaar) it. Parimelazhagar’s explanation is epistemic: insight not grounded in learning is accidental and unreliable, so it cannot be built upon. This anticipates Plato’s distinction in the Meno between true opinion and knowledge — right opinions are valuable but ‘run away’ unless tied down by reasoning, like the statues of Daedalus. The kural is harder-edged than some traditions would allow: Pirkei Avot’s ‘look not at the vessel but at what is in it’ pushes the other way, and Cassandra’s myth dramatizes the tragedy of truth rejected because of its source. The accuracy notes below mark these as contrasts.

tamil:
கல்லா ஒருவன் தகைமை தலைப்பெய்து
சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்.
transliteration:
Kallaa oruvan thagaimai thalaippeydhu
Sollaadach chorvu padum.
current_meaning: The self-esteem of an unlearned man will wither away as soon as he meets and converses with the learned.
elementary_explanation: Someone might think they’re very smart — until they start talking with people who have actually studied. Then, very quickly, it becomes clear how little they know, and their proud image falls apart.
university_explanation: Thagaimai is estimation or worth — here the self-estimation (or reputation) that the unlearned man carries; thalaippeydhu means ‘meeting, coming face to face’ (with the learned), and chorvu padum ‘will droop, fail’. The kural completes the logic of 402–403: the man who does not keep silent will be exposed in conversation. This is the drama of the Socratic elenchus, where confident interlocutors are shown in dialogue to lack what they claimed; Plato’s Phaedrus names the result ‘the show of wisdom without the reality’. The Mundaka and Katha Upanishads describe fools ‘wise in their own conceit’, and 1 Corinthians 8:2 compresses the diagnosis into a sentence. Dhammapada 63’s ‘fool who thinks himself wise’ is exactly the figure whose pride collapses here.

tamil:
உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர் அல்லால் பயவாக்
களரனையர் கல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Ularennum maaththiraiyar allaal payavaak
Kalaranaiyar kallaa thavar.
current_meaning: The unlearned can only be said to exist; beyond that, they are like barren saline land that yields nothing.
elementary_explanation: Some land is so salty that nothing grows on it, no matter how much rain falls. Valluvar says a person who never learns is like that land: they are there, alive, but nothing useful grows from them for themselves or anyone else.
university_explanation: Ularennum maaththiraiyar — ‘mere measure of existing’ — reduces the unlearned to bare presence. Kalar is saline or alkaline soil, proverbial in Tamil for barrenness; payavaa (‘unyielding’) insists on the absence of any fruit. The agricultural image makes learning the cultivation that turns land into field. Striking parallels exist: the Buddha’s Desana Sutta (SN 42.7) speaks of a field that is ‘salty’ and poor as the worst kind of soil; the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 79 compares recipients of knowledge to types of land, including barren land that neither holds water nor grows anything; Jeremiah 17:6 speaks of ‘a salt land and not inhabited’; Hesiod calls the man who neither thinks nor learns ‘unprofitable’; and Seneca’s ‘leisure without study is death… a tomb for the living man’ matches the Kural’s reduction of such a life to mere existence.

tamil:
நுண்மாண் நுழைபுலம் இல்லான் எழில்நலம்
மண்மாண் புனைபாவை யற்று.
transliteration:
Nunmaan nuzhaipulam illaan ezhilnalam
Manmaan punaipaavai yattru.
current_meaning: The fine looks of one who lacks subtle, penetrating understanding are like those of a beautifully painted doll made of clay.
elementary_explanation: A clay doll can be painted to look wonderful, but there is nothing inside it — it can’t think. Valluvar says a good-looking person who hasn’t developed a sharp, curious mind is like that doll: nice to look at, but empty.
university_explanation: Nunmaan nuzhaipulam — ‘subtle, excellent, penetrating intellect’ — names the kind of understanding that learning produces, able to enter into (nuzhai) fine distinctions. Its absence makes ezhil nalam (beauty, handsomeness) into manmaan punai paavai: a clay figure elaborately decorated. The contrast is surface versus interior. Aesop’s fox, finding an actor’s mask, puts it memorably: a beautiful head, but no brains. Chanakya Niti 3.8 is an almost perfect Sanskrit parallel — beauty, youth and noble birth without learning are like scentless kimshuka flowers. The Qur’an describes those whose ‘forms please you’ as ‘pieces of wood propped up’, and Proverbs likens beauty without discretion to a gold ring in a swine’s snout.

tamil:
நல்லார்கண் பட்ட வறுமையின் இன்னாதே
கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு.
transliteration:
Nallaarkan patta varumaiyin innaadhe
Kallaarkan patta thiru.
current_meaning: Wealth that falls into the hands of the unlearned brings more misery than poverty that falls upon the good.
elementary_explanation: It’s sad when good, wise people are poor. But Valluvar says it’s even worse when foolish, unlearned people get lots of money — because they don’t know how to use it well, and they can cause harm to themselves and everyone around them.
university_explanation: Innaadhu (painful, harmful) is the operative comparative: both situations are bad, but thiru (wealth, fortune) in the hands of the unlearned (kallaar) is worse than poverty befalling the good (nallaar). Parimelazhagar explains that the learned poor still do good and are not diminished, whereas the unlearned rich use wealth for harm. The verse belongs to Porul’s concern with statecraft: resources without wisdom are a public danger. Plato’s Euthydemus argues that wealth and other ‘goods’ are good only under the guidance of wisdom and become greater evils under ignorance; the Dhammapada says riches ruin the foolish; the Qur’an forbids handing property to the weak-minded; and Ecclesiastes laments folly set in great dignity.

tamil:
மேற்பிறந்தா ராயினும் கல்லாதார் கீழ்ப்பிறந்தும்
கற்றார் அனைத்திலர் பாடு.
transliteration:
Merpirandhaa raayinum kallaadhaar keezhppirandhum
Katraar anaiththilar paadu.
current_meaning: Though born in a high station, the unlearned do not have the worth of the learned who are born in a low one.
elementary_explanation: Some people think being born into an important family makes them better than others. Valluvar disagrees: a person from a humble family who has learned a lot is worth more than a high-born person who hasn’t learned anything. What you learn matters more than where you were born.
university_explanation: Merpirandhaar/keezhppirandhu (born high/born low) refers to the social hierarchy of birth in Valluvar’s world; paadu is dignity, worth or standing. The kural does not abolish hierarchy in theory but subordinates it to learning in practice, a notable move in a society structured by birth. The closest parallel is Mishnah Horayot 3:8: a mamzer who is a Torah scholar takes precedence over a High Priest who is ignorant. Buddhism’s Dhammapada 393 and the Vasala Sutta reject birth as the measure of a brahmin; the Upanishadic story of Satyakama Jabala shows a boy of unknown lineage accepted for his truthfulness; Plato’s myth of the metals places each child by the quality of soul, not parentage; and Ecclesiastes prefers a poor, wise youth to a foolish king.

tamil:
விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர் இலங்குநூல்
கற்றாரோடு ஏனை யவர்.
transliteration:
Vilangodu makkal anaiyar ilangunool
Katraarodu enai yavar.
current_meaning: As beasts are compared with human beings, so are the unlearned compared with those who have studied illustrious works.
elementary_explanation: Think of how different a person is from an animal. Valluvar says the difference between someone who has studied great books and someone who hasn’t is just as big. Learning is what makes us fully human.
university_explanation: The closing kural states the chapter’s thesis as a proportion: learned : unlearned :: humans : animals. Ilangu nool (‘shining, illustrious texts’) specifies that it is serious learning, not mere literacy, that marks the difference. The analogy draws on a long tradition, shared across cultures, that locates the distinctively human in reason and cultivated understanding. Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka 12 says one devoid of literature, music and art is a beast without tail and horns; Aristotle, asked how the educated differ from the uneducated, replied ‘as much as the living from the dead’; Psalm 49:20 compares the man in honour without understanding to the beasts that perish; the Qur’an (7:179) likens those who do not use their hearts to understand to livestock; and the Dhammapada’s man of little learning grows old ‘like a bull’.

tamil:
செல்வத்துள் செல்வம் செவிச்செல்வம் அச்செல்வம்
செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை.
transliteration:
Selvaththul selvam sevichchelvam achchelvam
Selvaththul ellaam thalai.
current_meaning: The wealth gained through the ear — the wisdom acquired by listening to the learned — is the wealth of wealth; of all kinds of wealth, it stands foremost.
elementary_explanation: People think of money, gold and houses as riches. Valluvar says the best treasure of all is what you gather by listening carefully to wise people. That kind of treasure goes into your mind, nobody can steal it, and it is worth more than any other.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with a deliberately repetitive line — செல்வம் occurs four times — which enacts its claim: among all the ‘wealths’, செவிச்செல்வம் (the wealth of the ear) is தலை, the head or chief. Placed in Porutpaal immediately after the chapters on learning (கல்வி) and its lack (கல்லாமை), this chapter supplements book-learning with கேள்வி, knowledge received orally from the learned — the dominant mode of transmitting knowledge in a largely oral culture. Parimelazhagar notes that hearing is especially valuable because it is available even to those who cannot study texts themselves, and because the ear receives the distilled result of another’s long learning. Calling it the ‘wealth’ of a treatise on polity is pointed: Valluvar ranks a cognitive possession above the material resources the rest of the book is about.

tamil:
செவிக்குணவு இல்லாத போழ்து சிறிது
வயிற்றுக்கும் ஈயப் படும்.
transliteration:
Sevikkunavu illaadha pozhdhu siridhu
Vayitrrukkum eeyap padum.
current_meaning: Only when there is no food for the ear (no instruction to listen to) should a little be given to the stomach as well.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you are hungry but a wise teacher is speaking. Valluvar says: keep listening first! Feed your ears with good words, and only when there is nothing more to hear, give your tummy a little food.
university_explanation: The kural introduces the governing metaphor of the chapter — hearing as food (செவிக்கு உணவு) — and inverts the ordinary priority of bodily needs. The ‘உம்’ in வயிற்றுக்கும் (‘to the stomach too’) and the qualifier சிறிது (‘a little’) make the stomach a secondary and moderate claimant. Commentators read this not as a call to starve but as a hierarchy: instruction, once lost, may not recur, whereas food can be taken any time. The metaphor links this chapter to the Indian notion of the body as sustained by food and the mind by speech, and anticipates 413 (hearers as those who eat ‘ear-food’) and 420 (those who know only the mouth’s taste).

tamil:
செவியுணவின் கேள்வி உடையார் அவியுணவின்
ஆன்றாரோடு ஒப்பர் நிலத்து.
transliteration:
Seviyunavin kelvi udaiyaar aviyunavin
Aandraarodu oppar nilaththu.
current_meaning: Those who possess learning gained by hearing — the food of the ear — are equal on earth to the gods, who feed on sacrificial oblations.
elementary_explanation: In old times people offered food to the gods through a sacred fire. Valluvar says people who ‘eat’ wise words through their ears are like gods living on earth.
university_explanation: A carefully balanced pair of compounds: செவியுணவு (ear-food) is set against அவியுணவு (oblation-food, havis), so that ‘those who have hearing’ are matched with ‘the exalted ones who eat oblations’ — the devas. Parimelazhagar glosses ஆன்றார் as the celestials; நிலத்து (‘on earth’) marks the hearers as terrestrial counterparts of the gods. The logic continues the food metaphor of 412: just as the gods are sustained by subtle offerings rather than gross food, the learned are sustained by subtle instruction. The kural thus elevates the listener’s status, not merely the value of what is heard.

tamil:
கற்றிலன் ஆயினும் கேட்க அஃதொருவற்கு
ஒற்கத்தின் ஊற்றாந் துணை.
transliteration:
Katrilan aayinum ketka aqdhoruvarku
Orkaththin ootraandh thunai.
current_meaning: Even if a person has not studied, let him listen to the learned; that hearing will be a supporting staff to him in times of weakness and adversity.
elementary_explanation: Maybe you never got to go to school or read many books. That’s okay — just listen to wise people! What you hear will be like a walking stick that holds you up when life gets hard.
university_explanation: Here Valluvar extends the chapter’s value to the unlettered: கற்றிலன் ஆயினும் (‘though he has not learned’) concedes lack of formal study, but கேட்க is an imperative — listening remains possible for everyone. ஒற்கம் means weakness, falling, or distress; ஊற்று is a prop or support (the same word recurs in 415 as ஊற்றுக்கோல், ‘supporting staff’). The kural thus democratises knowledge in an oral society: hearing is a route to wisdom for those without access to texts, and its value is practical — it sustains one when fortune slips.

tamil:
இழுக்கல் உடையுழி ஊற்றுக்கோல் அற்றே
ஒழுக்கம் உடையார்வாய்ச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Izhukkal udaiyuzhi ootrukkol atre
Ozhukkam udaiyaarvaaich chol.
current_meaning: The words from the mouths of the virtuous are like a supporting staff to one walking on slippery ground.
elementary_explanation: When you walk on a muddy, slippery path, a strong stick helps you not fall. Advice from good, honest people works the same way — it keeps you steady when life gets slippery.
university_explanation: The image is precise: இழுக்கல் is slipperiness (and by extension moral lapse), ஊற்றுக்கோல் a staff one leans on. The kural qualifies the source of hearing — not any speaker, but ஒழுக்கம் உடையார், those of upright conduct. Parimelazhagar emphasises that the words of the virtuous are trustworthy because their conduct confirms them, and that such words prevent a fall before it happens. The kural links the chapter to the earlier chapter on ஒழுக்கமுடைமை (conduct) and grounds the authority of what one hears in the moral character of the speaker.

tamil:
எனைத்தானும் நல்லவை கேட்க அனைத்தானும்
ஆன்ற பெருமை தரும்.
transliteration:
Enaiththaanum nallavai ketka anaiththaanum
Aandra perumai tharum.
current_meaning: Let one listen to good things, however little; even that little will bring full greatness.
elementary_explanation: You don’t have to listen to a huge lecture. Even hearing one small good idea is worth it, because even a little bit of goodness can make you a much better person.
university_explanation: The kural balances எனைத்தானும் (‘however little’) against அனைத்தானும் (‘to that very extent’), so that the benefit is proportionate to what is heard, yet always leads to ஆன்ற பெருமை — full, well-rounded greatness. Two conditions are embedded: the content must be நல்லவை (good things), and the act must be real listening. The couplet thus both encourages even small, occasional listening and implicitly warns against hearing what is not good — a selectivity that parallels many traditions’ counsel about what one lets into the ear.

tamil:
பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் பேதைமை சொல்லார் இழைத்துணர்ந்து
ஈண்டிய கேள்வி யவர்.
transliteration:
Pizhaiththunarndhum pedhaimai sollaar izhaiththunarndhu
Eendiya kelvi yavar.
current_meaning: Those who have examined things minutely and gathered abundant learning by hearing will not speak foolishly, even when they have misunderstood something.
elementary_explanation: Everyone makes mistakes sometimes. But a person who has listened carefully to lots of wise people won’t say silly things even when they get confused, because all that good listening keeps them careful.
university_explanation: The paired participles பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் (‘even having understood wrongly’) and இழைத்துணர்ந்து (‘having understood finely, as if threading’) frame the couplet. இழை (thread) suggests minute, careful examination; ஈண்டிய (‘amassed’) describes accumulated hearing. The kural is realistic: the learned may still err in perception, but their trained habit of mind prevents error from becoming foolish speech (பேதைமை). Hearing thus functions as a safeguard not of infallibility but of judgment.

tamil:
கேட்பினும் கேளாத் தகையவே கேள்வியால்
தோட்கப் படாத செவி.
transliteration:
Ketpinum kelaath thagaiyave kelviyaal
Thotkap padaadha sevi.
current_meaning: Ears that have not been pierced by instruction, though they hear sounds, are no better than deaf.
elementary_explanation: Your ears can hear noises all day, but if you never really listen to wise lessons, it’s almost like your ears don’t work. Real hearing means letting good lessons get inside.
university_explanation: The pun turns on கேள் (‘hear’): ears may கேட்பினும் (hear sounds) yet be கேளாத் தகைய (of the nature of not hearing, i.e., deaf) if not தோட்கப்பட்ட — ‘bored, pierced’ — by கேள்வி. The piercing alludes to the ear-boring ritual (and earrings) of Tamil custom: the true ornament and opening of the ear is instruction. The distinction between physiological hearing and receptive understanding is the heart of the kural and finds close echoes in prophetic and philosophical literature on ‘hearing without hearing’.

tamil:
நுணங்கிய கேள்வியர் அல்லார் வணங்கிய
வாயினர் ஆதல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Nunangiya kelviyar allaar vanangiya
Vaayinar aadhal aridhu.
current_meaning: It is hard for those who lack subtle, refined learning gained by hearing to possess humble, courteous speech.
elementary_explanation: People who have listened a lot to wise teachers usually speak kindly and humbly. People who haven’t listened much often find it hard to speak gently and politely.
university_explanation: Two adjectives govern the couplet: நுணங்கிய (fine, subtle) describes the quality of hearing, and வணங்கிய (bowed, humble) the quality of speech. The link is causal: refined hearing produces humility in speech, because the listener becomes aware of how much others know. Parimelazhagar reads வணங்கிய வாய் as speech that is modest and respectful. The kural thus connects the ear and the mouth: good speaking is an outcome of good listening — a theme echoed widely in wisdom literature that advises being quick to hear and slow to speak.

tamil:
செவியிற் சுவையுணரா வாயுணர்வின் மாக்கள்
அவியினும் வாழினும் என்.
transliteration:
Seviyir suvaiyunaraa vaayunarvin maakkal
Aviyinum vaazhinum en.
current_meaning: What does it matter whether they die or live — those beast-like people who know only the tastes of the mouth and not the tastes of the ear?
elementary_explanation: Some people only care about yummy food and never enjoy listening to wise words. Valluvar says, sharply, that such people live like animals — whether they live or die makes little difference to the world.
university_explanation: The closing kural returns to the food metaphor of 412–413 with a stinging contrast between செவியிற் சுவை (the ear’s taste) and வாயுணர்வு (mouth-knowledge, i.e., the palate). மாக்கள் denotes people without discernment — often glossed as ‘beast-like men’. The rhetorical question அவியினும் வாழினும் என் (‘whether they perish or live, what of it?’) declares their existence inconsequential. Some commentators take வாயுணர்வு as knowing only what one’s own mouth says, i.e., talkers who never listen; either way the chapter closes by denying full humanity to those who never cultivate hearing.

tamil:
அறிவற்றங் காக்குங் கருவி செறுவார்க்கும்
உள்ளழிக்க லாகா அரண்.
transliteration:
Arivatrang kaakkum karuvi seruvaarkkum
Ullazhikka laakaa aran.
current_meaning: Wisdom is a weapon that guards a person against ruin; it is also an inner fortress that even enemies cannot breach or destroy.
elementary_explanation: Imagine having a shield and a castle that nobody can ever take away from you. Valluvar says good sense is exactly that. It protects you from making ruinous mistakes, and no enemy can break into it, because it lives inside you.
university_explanation: The couplet sets up the governing metaphor of the chapter: arivu is both karuvi (an instrument or weapon) and aran (a fortress). The word அற்றம் (atram) means destruction, ruin, or a vulnerable moment of exposure. Parimelazhagan reads arivu as the faculty that keeps a person from falling into ruin. The second line moves the fortress inward: உள் (ul) is 'inside', so this is a stronghold that attackers (செறுவார், 'those who hate') cannot tear down from within. Placing the chapter in Porutpal is significant. For a king, forts, armies, and treasuries are external defences that can be besieged or bribed away, while discernment cannot be captured. The pairing of 'weapon' and 'wall' covers both active and passive defence. Stoic thought makes the same move with Marcus Aurelius's 'inner citadel', and the Dhammapada's image of the mind fortified like a city is similar.

tamil:
சென்ற இடத்தால் செலவிடா தீதொரீஇ
நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்ப தறிவு.
transliteration:
Sendra idaththaal selavidaa theethoreei
Nandrinpaal uyppa tharivu.
current_meaning: Wisdom is not letting the mind run wherever it wanders. It holds the mind back from evil and steers it toward the good.
elementary_explanation: Your mind is a bit like a puppy that wants to run off in every direction. Wisdom is the leash. It stops the puppy from running into trouble and gently pulls it toward good things.
university_explanation: Here arivu is defined by its function over the mind (implied as the subject). சென்ற இடத்தால் செலவிடா means 'not letting it go wherever it goes'. தீது ஒரீஇ means 'removing it from evil', and நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது means 'leading it toward the good'. Three movements are involved: restraint, withdrawal, and redirection. Wisdom is therefore not only knowing the good but actively governing attention and desire. Parimelazhagan glosses the object as the mind driven by the five senses. The image matches Indian and Greek charioteer models of the psyche (Katha Upanishad, Plato's Phaedrus), where intelligence holds the reins of the senses. The Buddhist 'fletcher straightening the arrow' image is similar. The Kural is notably positive: wisdom does not simply suppress the mind, it 'leads' it (uyppathu) somewhere better.

tamil:
எப்பொருள் யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும் அப்பொருள்
மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்ப தறிவு.
transliteration:
Epporul yaaryaarvaaik ketpinum apporul
Meipporul kaanpa tharivu.
current_meaning: Whatever you hear, and from whomever you hear it, wisdom is seeing the real truth of that matter.
