elementary_explanation: Sometimes people believe something just because a famous or important person said it. Sometimes they ignore something true because someone they don't like said it. Valluvar says a wise person looks at what was said and asks, 'Is this actually true?', no matter who said it.
university_explanation: This is among the most frequently quoted Kurals, often cited as an early statement of critical thinking. The repetition யார்யார் ('whoever, whoever') stresses that the speaker's status, reputation, or hostility is irrelevant. The contrast between பொருள் (porul, the thing said or its surface content) and மெய்ப்பொருள் (meipporul, its true substance) separates what is asserted from what is real. Two errors are ruled out. One is deference to authority, accepting a claim because of who said it. The other is the ad hominem, rejecting it for the same reason. The Kural is less radical than modern empiricism, because it assumes the truth can be discerned through judgment. Still, its location of arivu in the evaluation of claims, not in the collecting of them, anticipates the Buddhist Kalama Sutta and Aristotle's 'truth above friends'. For a king in Porutpal, this is also advice about handling the reports of ministers, spies, and flatterers.

tamil:
எண்பொருள வாகச் செலச்சொல்லித் தான்பிறர்வாய்
நுண்பொருள் காண்ப தறிவு.
transliteration:
Enporula vaagach selachcholli thaanpirarvaai
Nunporul kaanpa tharivu.
current_meaning: Wisdom is speaking so that your meaning is easily grasped and sinks into the listener's mind, and also perceiving the subtle meaning in what others say.
elementary_explanation: A wise person does two things with words. When they talk, they explain things so clearly that others understand easily. When they listen, they catch even the small, hidden points in what others are saying.
university_explanation: The couplet describes wisdom in communication as running in two directions. In speaking, எண்பொருள ஆக means 'so that the meaning is easy' and செலச் சொல்லி means 'speaking so that it goes in', that is, lodges in the listener. In listening, நுண்பொருள் காண்பது means 'seeing the subtle or fine meaning' in another's words. The contrast between எண் (easy, simple) and நுண் (subtle, fine) is deliberate. The wise person simplifies when giving and refines when receiving. This is a sophisticated account of communicative intelligence, close to what classical rhetoric called knowing one's audience (Plato's Phaedrus) and to hermeneutic charity in interpreting others. For rulers and ministers, the Porutpal setting, it is practical advice: make your orders clear, and read the unstated intentions of envoys and courtiers.

tamil:
உலகம் தழீஇய தொட்பம் மலர்தலும்
கூம்பலும் இல்ல தறிவு.
transliteration:
Ulagam thazheeiya thotpam malarthalum
Koombalum illa tharivu.
current_meaning: Excellence lies in befriending the worthy of the world. Wisdom lies in keeping that friendship steady, without first blossoming out and then closing up.
elementary_explanation: Some people are super friendly one day and cold the next, like a flower that opens in the morning and shuts at night. Valluvar says it is smart to make friends with good people. It is wise to stay the same kind friend every day, not hot one day and cold the next.
university_explanation: This is the most debated couplet in the chapter. ஒட்பம் (otpam) means excellence or sagacity, and உலகம் (ulagam, 'the world') is read by Parimelazhagan and most commentators as 'the great ones of the world' (uyarndhor). The first half therefore says that true excellence is to befriend the eminent. The second half uses a flower image: மலர்தல் (blooming, opening) and கூம்பல் (closing, as a flower does at dusk). Wisdom is keeping that friendship constant, neither over-effusive at the start nor withdrawing later. Some modern readers (e.g. Karunanidhi, Mu. Varadarasan) take the flower image more broadly as emotional equanimity in joy and sorrow. Both readings stress stability: arivu produces steadiness of disposition, especially in relationships. Aristotle's view that friendships of the good endure because goodness endures is a close parallel.

tamil:
எவ்வ துறைவது உலகம் உலகத்தோடு
அவ்வ துறைவ தறிவு.
transliteration:
Evva thuraivathu ulagam ulagaththodu
Avva thuraiva tharivu.
current_meaning: Wisdom is living in harmony with the world: conducting oneself as the world (the worthy) conducts itself.
elementary_explanation: Every place has its own ways of doing things. A wise person notices how good people around them behave and fits in with them, instead of being odd or rude just to stand out.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on the parallel எவ்வது / அவ்வது ('in whatever way / in that way') and on the verb உறைதல் (to dwell or abide). Wisdom is to abide with the world in the way the world abides. As in 425, Parimelazhagan takes ulagam to mean the uyarndhor, the worthy or great of the world, not the crowd. The Kural is therefore not a call to conformity with the majority but to conduct in step with the accepted norms of the good. It still carries a real social insight: discernment includes reading context and custom and not acting eccentrically. This complements 423. There, wisdom judges claims independently; here, wisdom adapts one's conduct to the settled ways of good society. Parallels range from the Talmudic 'never deviate from local custom' to Paul's 'all things to all men' and Descartes's provisional maxim of following his country's customs.

tamil:
அறிவுடையார் ஆவ தறிவார் அறிவிலார்
அஃதறி கல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Arivudaiyaar aava tharivaar arivilaar
Aqdhari kallaa thavar.
current_meaning: The wise know beforehand what is going to happen; the unwise are those who cannot know it.
elementary_explanation: If you see dark clouds, you know rain is coming and take an umbrella. A wise person is good at spotting what is going to happen next, while a foolish person gets caught by surprise every time.
university_explanation: This couplet defines wisdom and its lack by one criterion: foresight. ஆவது அறிவார் means 'they know what will come to be'. The second line mirrors it: the unwise are precisely those who cannot know that (அஃது அறிகல்லாதவர்). Commentators take ஆவது to mean the outcome or consequence of present actions and circumstances, not supernatural prophecy. Arivu here is predictive practical judgment, the ability to read causes forward to their effects. The Talmudic definition 'who is wise? One who sees what will be born' is almost a translation. Aristotle's phronesis includes deliberating well about what conduces to the good in the long run, and Hesiod's Prometheus (forethought) and Epimetheus (afterthought) personify the Kural's opposition. The couplet also prepares for 429, where foresight becomes protection.

tamil:
அஞ்சுவ தஞ்சாமை பேதைமை அஞ்சுவது
அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Anjuva thanjaamai pethaimai anjuvathu
Anjal arivaar thozhil.
current_meaning: Not fearing what ought to be feared is folly; fearing what ought to be feared is the way of the wise.
elementary_explanation: Being brave does not mean being scared of nothing. A person who isn't afraid of touching a hot stove or running across a busy road is not brave, just foolish. Wise people are careful about the things that really are dangerous.
university_explanation: The couplet rests on the repeated verb அஞ்சு (to fear) in a tight chiastic pattern. அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சாமை ('not fearing the fearworthy') is பேதைமை (folly), and அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் ('fearing the fearworthy') is the practice (தொழில்) of the wise. Fear is treated not as a weakness to overcome but as an emotion to calibrate. Commentators apply it to wrongdoing, the anger of the powerful, and real dangers. This is almost exactly Aristotle's doctrine of courage as a mean: the brave person fears the right things in the right way, and fearlessness toward everything is rashness. The Dhammapada (317) and Proverbs (14:16) make the same point. In the Porutpal context, a king who fears nothing, not even enemies, public anger, or his own misdeeds, is a danger to the state.

tamil:
எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்க் கில்லை
அதிர வருவதோர் நோய்.
transliteration:
Ethirathaak kaakkum arivinaark killai
Athira varuvathor noi.
current_meaning: For the wise who guard in advance against what is coming, there is no calamity that strikes them so as to make them tremble.
elementary_explanation: If you know a storm is coming and you close the windows and bring in your toys, the storm can't really hurt you. Wise people prepare ahead of time, so when trouble comes it doesn't shake them.
university_explanation: Building on 427 (knowing what will come), this couplet adds action: எதிரதாக் காக்கும் means 'guarding against it as something ahead', that is, protecting oneself before a danger arrives. The result: இல்லை அதிர வருவதோர் நோய் ('there is no affliction that comes so as to make them shudder'). நோய் (noi) literally means disease but is used broadly for suffering or calamity, and அதிர (to shake or tremble) vividly describes the shock of being unprepared. The claim is not that the wise escape every misfortune but that nothing catches them off guard. This parallels the Stoic premeditatio malorum, the Panchatantra fable of the three fish, and Jesus's parable of the house built on rock. It links back to 421's image of arivu as a protective weapon.

tamil:
அறிவுடையார் எல்லா முடையார் அறிவிலார்
என்னுடைய ரேனும் இலர்.
transliteration:
Arivudaiyaar ellaa mudaiyaar arivilaar
Ennudaiya renum ilar.
current_meaning: Those who possess wisdom possess everything; those who lack wisdom possess nothing, whatever else they may have.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone with a huge pile of money but no sense. They would probably lose it all or use it badly. Someone with good sense can build up whatever they need. Valluvar says good sense is the one thing that counts as having everything.
university_explanation: The chapter ends with a sweeping summary built on the verb உடைமை (possession) that gives the chapter its title. அறிவுடையார் எல்லாம் உடையார் means 'the possessors of wisdom are possessors of all'. என்னுடையரேனும் இலர் means 'whatever they possess, they have nothing'. The point is that wisdom is the meta-possession that makes other possessions useful and secure. Without it, wealth, power, and allies are squandered or turned against their holder. It is striking that this appears in Porutpal, the book on wealth and statecraft: Valluvar ranks arivu above porul (wealth) itself. The Talmud's 'if you have acquired knowledge, what do you lack?' and Socrates's argument in the Euthydemus that wisdom is the only unconditional good are close parallels. Solomon's story, in which he chooses wisdom and receives everything else too, dramatises the same claim.

tamil:
செருக்குஞ் சினமும் சிறுமையும் இல்லார்
பெருக்கம் பெருமித நீர்த்து.
transliteration:
Serukkunj chinamum sirumaiyum illaar
Perukkam perumitha neerththu.
current_meaning: The prosperity of those who are free from arrogance, anger, and base desire carries real dignity and is held in honour.
elementary_explanation: Some people get rich and then turn bossy, angry, and greedy for low pleasures. This kural says that when someone does well in life but stays humble, calm, and clean-minded, their success is the kind people truly respect.
university_explanation: The chapter opens by naming three faults (குற்றம்) a ruler must purge: செருக்கு (arrogance, the swelling of self that success breeds), சினம் (anger), and சிறுமை (literally ‘smallness’; Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan gloss it as காமம், base lust or petty desire). The claim is conditional and political: பெருக்கம் (increase, prosperity) only becomes பெருமிதம் (dignity, honourable greatness) when these three are absent. Wealth and power are morally neutral amplifiers; what they amplify is character. The triadic diagnosis of pride, anger and desire as the roots of ruin is one of the most widely shared moral analyses across ancient traditions, from the Gita’s ‘demoniac’ qualities to the Mishnah’s list of things that ‘put a man out of the world’.

tamil:
இவறலும் மாண்பிறந்த மானமும் மாணா
உவகையும் ஏதம் இறைக்கு.
transliteration:
Ivaralum maanbirandha maanamum maanaa
Uvakaiyum yedham iraikku.
current_meaning: Avarice, pride that has lost all worth, and unseemly delight are faults that harm a ruler.
elementary_explanation: A leader should not be stingy, should not be proud about the wrong things, and should not enjoy things that are low or harmful. This kural says those three habits are dangers for anyone in charge.
university_explanation: Valluvar adds a second triad specific to kingship (இறை, ‘the ruler’): இவறல் (miserliness, refusing to give what should be given), மாண்பு இறந்த மானம் (a sense of honour that has ‘died to excellence’, i.e. touchy pride over the wrong things; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as refusing to bow to the worthy out of pride of office), and மாணா உவகை (joy in what is unworthy). ஏதம் means harm or fault. Each is a perversion of a legitimate royal trait: prudence with wealth decays into avarice, dignity into vanity, and a king’s pleasures into indulgence. Miserliness returns in Kurals 437 and 438 as the gravest of all faults, so this couplet frames the chapter’s political core: a ruler’s private vices become public dangers.

tamil:
தினைத்துணையாங் குற்றம் வரினும் பனைத்துணையாக்
கொள்வர் பழிநாணு வார்.
transliteration:
Thinaiththunaiyaang kutram varinum panaiththunaiyaak
Kolvar pazhinaanu vaar.
current_meaning: Those who dread disgrace, even if a fault as small as a millet seed arises in them, will treat it as though it were as large as a palmyra tree.
elementary_explanation: A millet seed is tiny, and a palm tree is huge. People who really care about doing right treat even a tiny mistake as if it were a giant one, so they fix it straight away instead of letting it grow.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a vivid scale contrast between தினை (foxtail millet, among the smallest grains) and பனை (the palmyra palm, among the tallest trees). பழிநாணுவார், ‘those who are ashamed before blame’, are defined not by having no faults but by how they perceive them: they magnify their own errors in their own eyes. This is a moral psychology of vigilance. Shame (நாண்) works here as a protective faculty, the Tamil counterpart of Greek aidōs, that makes a small lapse feel intolerable before it can grow. The commentators divide on whether the sense is ‘they grieve over it as if it were huge’ (Puliyur Kesikan) or ‘they guard against it as if it were huge’ (Varadarasan, Karunanidhi); both readings share the principle of disproportionate self-scrutiny.

tamil:
குற்றமே காக்க பொருளாகக் குற்றமே
அற்றந் தரூஉம் பகை.
transliteration:
Kutrame kaakka porulaakak kutrame
Atran tharooum pakai.
current_meaning: Make it your chief aim to guard against faults, for it is fault itself that is the enemy that brings ruin.
elementary_explanation: We often worry about enemies outside us. This kural says the most dangerous enemy is a bad habit or mistake inside ourselves, because that is what can truly destroy us. So guarding against our own faults should be our main job.
university_explanation: The repetition of குற்றமே (‘fault itself’) in both lines is emphatic: the ēkāram singles out fault, not external foes, as the true enemy. பொருளாக can be read as ‘as the essential aim’ or, with a pun on பொருள் (wealth, the theme of the whole Porutpāl), ‘as though it were your treasure’: guarding against faults is to be protected like wealth. அற்றம் means ruin or destruction, and தரூஉம் is the prolonged (alapedai) form of தரும், ‘that which brings’. (The two digitised editions consulted print ‘த்ரூஉம்’, a typographical slip for தரூஉம்.) The political reading (Solomon Pappaiah) is that a state is destroyed less by invading armies than by the ruler’s own moral failings, which is the governing thesis of this chapter.

tamil:
வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான் வாழ்க்கை எரிமுன்னர்
வைத்தூறு போலக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Varumunnark kaavaathaan vaazhkkai erimunnar
Vaiththooru polak kedum.
current_meaning: The life of one who does not guard against faults before they arrive will perish like a heap of straw placed before a fire.
elementary_explanation: Dry straw near a fire catches in a flash. This kural says that if you don’t protect yourself from mistakes before they happen, your life can go up in flames just as quickly.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a pointed parallel of two முன்னர் (‘before’): வருமுன்னர் (before [the fault] comes) and எரிமுன்னர் (before the fire). Failure to act in the first ‘before’ puts one in the second. வைத்தூறு is a stack of straw (வைக்கோல் போர்), the most combustible of village materials, so the image stresses how sudden and total the ruin is once prevention has failed. This is the chapter’s case for preventive rather than corrective vigilance: once a fault has taken hold, correction may already be too late. The same principle appears in Valluvar’s wider political thought on foresight (compare Kural 442 in the next chapter, which praises counsellors who guard against troubles before they arrive).

tamil:
தன்குற்றம் நீக்கிப் பிறர்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்
என்குற்ற மாகும் இறைக்கு.
transliteration:
Thankutram neekkip pirarkutrang kaankirpin
Enkutra maakum iraikku.
current_meaning: If a ruler first removes his own faults and only then examines the faults of others, what fault could ever befall him?
elementary_explanation: It is easy to spot what others are doing wrong. This kural says a good leader first looks at and fixes their own mistakes, and only then points out other people’s. A leader who does that has nothing to be blamed for.
university_explanation: This is the chapter’s central statement of self-scrutiny and its logic is sequential: தன்குற்றம் நீக்கி (having removed one’s own fault) comes before பிறர்குற்றம் காண் (seeing others’ faults). The verb காண்கிற்பின் (‘if one is able to see’) implies that judging others rightly is a capacity earned by self-correction. The closing rhetorical question, என்குற்றம் ஆகும் இறைக்கு (‘what fault would there be for the king?’), expects the answer ‘none’. For a ruler whose office is to judge, this is the ethics of legitimate authority: the right to correct others rests on having corrected oneself. The couplet is the Tamil counterpart of the ‘mote and beam’ teaching and of the fable of the two wallets, but it is framed positively as a programme for governance rather than as a rebuke to hypocrisy.

tamil:
செயற்பால செய்யா திவறியான் செல்வம்
உயற்பால தன்றிக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Seyarpaala seyyaa thivariyaan selvam
Uyarpaala thandrik kedum.
current_meaning: The wealth of the miser who does not do what ought to be done with it will not endure; it will perish without being of use.
elementary_explanation: Money is meant to be used for good things: helping people, caring for family, doing what is right. This kural says that if someone just sits on their money out of stinginess, it ends up wasted and lost anyway.
university_explanation: செயற்பால (‘things that ought to be done’) are the proper uses of wealth, which Valluvar elsewhere lists as giving, enjoyment and public works; இவறியான் is the one who clings (from இவறு, to hoard or be miserly). உயற்பாலது அன்றி means ‘without the quality of surviving / being saved’: hoarded wealth has no future. The argument is not only moral but practical: wealth that is not put to use is exposed to theft, confiscation and decay, and so the miser loses both the good he could have done and the wealth itself. The couplet returns to இவறல் from Kural 432 and prepares for 438’s verdict that miserliness is the worst of all faults.

tamil:
பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை எற்றுள்ளும்
எண்ணப் படுவதொன் றன்று.
transliteration:
Patrullam ennum ivaranmai etrullum
Ennap paduvathon randru.
current_meaning: The miserliness called a grasping heart is not to be counted among other faults at all; it stands apart as a fault beyond them all.
elementary_explanation: This kural says that stinginess, a heart that grabs and won’t let go, is not just one bad habit on a list. It is in a class of its own, worse than all the others.
university_explanation: பற்றுள்ளம் (‘a clinging heart’) defines இவறன்மை (miserliness) as a disposition of attachment, not merely an act of not giving. The phrase எற்றுள்ளும் எண்ணப்படுவது ஒன்று அன்று (‘it is not a thing to be counted among any [faults]’) is deliberately ambiguous: Mu. Varadarasan reads it as ‘a separate fault that cannot be counted along with others’, and Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi read it as ‘the most terrible of all faults’. Either way it is the chapter’s climax on avarice, which has now appeared three times (432, 437, 438). The ruler-centred reading matters: a stingy king starves the gifts, rewards and public works on which loyalty and prosperity depend, so his avarice spreads into every other failure.

tamil:
வியவற்க எஞ்ஞான்றும் தன்னை நயவற்க
நன்றி பயவா வினை.
transliteration:
Viyavarka enjnaandrum thannai nayavarka
Nandri payavaa vinai.
current_meaning: Never, at any time, admire yourself; and never desire deeds that bring no good.
elementary_explanation: Being impressed with yourself makes you stop noticing your mistakes. This kural gives two simple rules: never be too proud of yourself, and don’t want to do things that don’t do any good.
university_explanation: Two prohibitions run in parallel: வியவற்க (do not wonder at, marvel at) with தன்னை (oneself), and நயவற்க (do not desire) with நன்றி பயவா வினை (deeds that yield no good). எஞ்ஞான்றும் (‘at any time’) makes the first absolute: even at the height of success, self-admiration is forbidden. The two are causally linked. Self-admiration blinds a person to their own faults, which undoes the self-scrutiny of Kural 436, and a self-admiring ruler is the one most easily drawn into vain, unprofitable projects. Solomon Pappaiah reads the second clause politically: a ruler should not want to do what does not benefit the country and its governance.

tamil:
காதல காதல் அறியாமை உய்க்கிற்பின்
ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல்.
transliteration:
Kaadhala kaadhal ariyaamai uykkirpin
Edhila edhilaar nool.
current_meaning: If one can enjoy what one loves without others knowing one’s desires, the schemes of one’s enemies will come to nothing.
elementary_explanation: If everyone knows exactly what you want most, people who wish you harm can use that to trick you. This kural says a wise leader keeps their wishes private, so enemies have nothing to use against them.
university_explanation: The couplet uses doubled words for effect: காதல காதல் (‘the things one loves, [and] one’s love’) and ஏதில ஏதிலார் (‘come to nothing, [the plans of] strangers/enemies’). ஏதிலார் means those unrelated or hostile, and நூல் here means their ‘science’ or stratagems, the craft by which they plot. உய்க்கிற்பின் (‘if one is able to experience/carry out’) makes the condition discretion, not renunciation: the ruler may pursue his desires, but must not let them be known. The logic ties the chapter together. A known weakness or appetite is itself a fault (குற்றம்) in the strategic sense, a gap in the armour. By closing the chapter this way, Valluvar moves from moral self-correction to political self-guarding: the ruler must hide from enemies the very desires that could be used to exploit him.

chapter_title: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
tamil:
அறனறிந்து மூத்த அறிவுடையார் கேண்மை
திறனறிந்து தேர்ந்து கொளல்.
transliteration:
Aranarindhu mootha arivudaiyaar kenmai
Thiranarindhu therndhu kolal.
current_meaning: Learn the right way to win it, weigh carefully, and then secure the friendship of those who know dharma and are mature in wisdom.
elementary_explanation: Some people know what is right and have learned a lot from long experience. This kural says: find people like that, think carefully about who they really are, and then work to make them your friends and helpers.
university_explanation: The chapter opens by fixing three qualifications for the ‘great’ (periyar): they know aram (virtue/duty), they are ‘mootha’ (ripened, whether in age or in understanding), and they possess arivu (knowledge). The verb structure is significant: ‘thiran arindhu’ (knowing the method) and ‘therndhu’ (having examined) both precede ‘kolal’ (taking). Friendship with the wise is not an accident of proximity but a deliberate, tested acquisition — a theme Valluvar develops later in the chapters on friendship (79–83). Parimelazhagar notes that this counsel is addressed first to the king, for whom advisers are an instrument of rule, but it generalises readily to anyone: one’s judgment is only as good as the judgment of those one keeps close.

chapter_title: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
tamil:
உற்றநோய் நீக்கி உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும்
பெற்றியார்ப் பேணிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Utranoi neekki uraaamai murkaakkum
Petriyaarp penik kolal.
current_meaning: Cherish and secure as your own those who have the ability to remove troubles that have already come and to guard you in advance against troubles yet to come.
elementary_explanation: Some wise people can help you fix a problem you already have, and can also warn you about problems before they happen. This kural says: treat people like that with great care and keep them close.
university_explanation: ‘Noi’ literally means disease, but here it stands for any affliction — political, financial, or personal. The couplet distinguishes two functions of the wise counselor: the remedial (utra noi neekki, removing the affliction already suffered) and the preventive (uraamai murkaakkum, guarding beforehand against what has not yet arrived). The latter is the rarer gift, since it requires foresight. ‘Petriyaar’ denotes those who possess this capacity as a settled quality, and ‘penik kolal’ (cherishing and holding) implies that such people must be honored and maintained, not merely consulted when convenient.

chapter_title: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
tamil:
அரியவற்று ளெல்லாம் அரிதே பெரியாரைப்
பேணித் தமராக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Ariyavatru lellaam aridhe periyaaraip
Penith thamaraak kolal.
current_meaning: Of all rare things, the rarest is to honor great men and make them one’s own kin.
elementary_explanation: Many things in life are hard to get. But this kural says the hardest and most precious thing of all is to have truly great people treat you like family, because you have honored and cared for them.
university_explanation: The superlative construction ‘ariyavatrul ellaam aridhe’ (rarest among all rare things) places the friendship of the great above wealth, armies, and territory, all of which are also ‘rare’ in the Porutpaal. The key word is ‘thamar’ — one’s own people, kin. Valluvar is not describing hiring an expert but transforming a great person into someone bound to you by affection and loyalty; ‘peni’ (having cherished) marks the reciprocity required. The rarity has two sources: the great are few, and they cannot be commanded — they must be won.

chapter_title: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
tamil:
தம்மிற் பெரியார் தமரா ஒழுகுதல்
வன்மையு ளெல்லாந் தலை.
transliteration:
Thammir periyaar thamaraa ozhukudhal
Vanmaiyu lellaan thalai.
current_meaning: To conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself become one’s own is the foremost of all strengths.
elementary_explanation: Being strong isn’t just about muscles or money. This kural says the best kind of strength is behaving in a way that makes people who are wiser and better than you want to be on your side.
university_explanation: ‘Thammil periyaar’ — those greater than oneself — is the pointed phrase. Rulers and the powerful typically surround themselves with inferiors who flatter; Valluvar calls instead for the humility to keep superiors as intimates. ‘Ozhukudhal’ (conducting oneself) makes this a matter of sustained behavior, not a single act. Calling it the chief of all ‘vanmai’ (strengths) reframes power itself: the strength that multiplies other strengths is the ability to attract and retain better minds.

chapter_title: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
tamil:
சூழ்வார்கண் ணாக ஒழுகலான் மன்னவன்
சூழ்வாரைச் சூழ்ந்து கொளல்.
transliteration:
Soozhvaarkan naaka ozhukalaan mannavan
Soozhvaaraich soozhndhu kolal.
current_meaning: Since a king must conduct himself with his counselors as his eyes, he should select those counselors after careful deliberation.
elementary_explanation: A king can’t see everything himself, so his advisers are like his eyes. If your eyes are bad, you can’t see clearly. So this kural says a leader must think very carefully before choosing advisers.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on the root ‘soozh’ (to deliberate, plan): ‘soozhvaar’ are those who deliberate, and the king must ‘soozhndhu’ (deliberate) in choosing them. The wordplay enacts the argument — deliberation is needed to choose the deliberators. ‘Kan aaka’ (as eyes) is the governing metaphor: a king perceives his realm largely through ministers’ reports and judgments, so their quality determines the accuracy of his vision. The later chapter on ministers (Amaichu, ch. 64) builds on this principle.

chapter_title: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
tamil:
தக்கா ரினத்தனாய்த் தானொழுக வல்லானைச்
செற்றார் செயக்கிடந்த தில்.
transliteration:
Thakkaa rinaththanaaith thaanozhuka vallaanaich
Chetraar seyakkidandha thil.
current_meaning: There is nothing his enemies can do to one who is able to live as a member of the company of the worthy.
elementary_explanation: If you stay close to good and wise people and act like one of them, your enemies will find there is nothing they can do to hurt you.
university_explanation: ‘Thakkaar inaththan’ — one who belongs to the fellowship of the worthy — moves from the friendship of individuals to membership in a circle. ‘Thaan ozhuka vallaan’ (one able himself to conduct himself so) implies that belonging requires one’s own discipline; the worthy will not keep company with the unworthy. The consequence is framed in the negative with total scope: ‘setraar seyak kidandhadhu il’ — there remains nothing for enemies to do. The protection is both practical (good advice closes vulnerabilities) and reputational (a ruler surrounded by the virtuous is hard to isolate).

chapter_title: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
tamil:
இடிக்குந் துணையாரை ஆள்வாரை யாரே
கெடுக்குந் தகைமை யவர்.
transliteration:
Idikkun thunaiyaarai aalvaarai yaare
Kedukkun thakaimai yavar.
current_meaning: Who can ruin those who keep as companions men able to rebuke them?
elementary_explanation: A good friend will tell you when you are doing something wrong, even if it hurts to hear. This kural asks: if you keep friends like that close, who could ever bring you down?
university_explanation: ‘Idikkum’ means to strike or rebuke — Parimelazhagar glosses it as reproving the king when he errs. The couplet is a rhetorical question that assumes its answer: none. What protects the ruler is not deference but correction. The idea is especially pointed in a political treatise, since rulers are the persons least likely to hear criticism. ‘Aalvaar’ (those who rule / keep) suggests the king must actively maintain such critics in his service rather than merely tolerate them.

chapter_title: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
tamil:
இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ஏமரா மன்னன்
கெடுப்பா ரிலானுங் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Idippaarai illaadha emaraa mannan
Keduppaa rilaanung kedum.
current_meaning: The unguarded king who has no one to rebuke him will perish even when there is no one to destroy him.
elementary_explanation: A king with nobody brave enough to tell him he’s wrong is like someone walking without looking. Even if no enemy attacks him, he will trip over his own mistakes and fall.
university_explanation: This is the converse of 447. ‘Emaraa’ means unprotected or unsafeguarded — the missing protection is precisely the rebuker. The striking phrase ‘keduppaar ilaanum kedum’ (perishes even without destroyers) locates the source of ruin inside: unchecked error compounds until it destroys. Valluvar thus anticipates a well-known insight of political thought — that autocrats surrounded by yes-men fall by their own misjudgments more often than by foreign conquest.

chapter_title: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
tamil:
முதலிலார்க் கூதிய மில்லை மதலையாஞ்
சார்பிலார்க் கில்லை நிலை.
transliteration:
Mudhalilaark kooodhiya millai madhalaiyaanj
Chaarbilaark killai nilai.
current_meaning: Just as there is no profit for those without capital, there is no stability for those without the support of the worthy to prop them up.
elementary_explanation: You can’t earn money from a business if you have no money to start it. In the same way, you can’t stay steady and safe in life if you have no wise people to lean on.
university_explanation: An economic analogy fitting the Porutpaal: ‘mudhal’ (capital) is to ‘oodhiyam’ (profit) as ‘saarbu’ (support) is to ‘nilai’ (stability). ‘Madhalai’ is a prop or supporting beam — the support of the great is the load-bearing pillar of a leader’s position. The analogy implies that alliance with the worthy is not an optional extra but the principal on which all further returns are earned.

chapter_title: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
tamil:
பல்லார் பகைகொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்தே
நல்லார் தொடர்கை விடல்.
transliteration:
Pallaar pakaikolalir paththaduththa theemaiththe
Nallaar thodarkai vidal.
current_meaning: To give up the friendship of the good is ten times more harmful than to incur the enmity of many.
elementary_explanation: Having lots of enemies is bad. But this kural says losing the friendship of good people is ten times worse than that.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with a calculus: ‘paththu aduththa’ (ten times over) compares two harms. Enmity from many (pallaar) is external and can be countered; abandonment of good friends (nallaar thodarkai vidal) removes the very counsel and support by which enemies are countered — so it multiplies every other danger. The verb ‘vidal’ (letting go) places responsibility on the one who drops such friendships, whether through pride, neglect, or preference for flatterers.
